In this lecture I'm going to give you an outline for the rest of this course. First I want to give you a brief summary of what pytorch is all about. In case you've had previous experience with TensorFlow or other deep learning libraries such as the theano.. So in the beginning there was Theano. Theano was a significant improvement over what was being done previously for two major reasons. Number one for reasons you'll learn about later writing neural network that works from scratch involves doing a lot of Matrix calculus by hand and then copying those equations into code for those of you who took my first deep learning course. You know how difficult this can be. The Theano library was the first to innovate in this area using automatic differentiation or auto diff for sure what that means is you don't have to write down Calculus Equations since the computer will do that for you. And number two there's a lot of math that has to happen in a neuron that work. And this takes a lot of time meaning you'd have to wait hours or even days or weeks to train your neural network. The Theano Library was the first to innovate in this area by making use of GPUs which were originally designed to improve the performance of P.C. Games. One of the downsides of older libraries such as the Theano is that you have to build everything by yourself. This can really slow you down especially if it's your first time writing certain components. You not only have to write each component on your own you'll also have to worry about them being right. If any single component you wrote is wrong then it could make your entire program fail. On top of that in the previous years it was announced that the Theano Library would no longer be maintained. What about TensorFlow ? TensorFlow is a pretty popular library, thanks to the fact that it's backed by Google who at this point kind of run the Internet TensorFlow used to be really messy. In fact probably more so than Theano But now in version 2.0 it uses the Keras API which is the total opposite. It's very high level and very simple but there is a downside to very high level and very simple APIs. They make it very easy to do common things but hard to do uncommon things. PyTorch on the other hand has been slowly gaining adoption in the field of deep learning thanks to the fact that it's relatively easy to do common things and still easy to do uncommon things. For this reason it's been extremely popular in the research community who by definition do lots of uncommon things. That's their job after all. PyTorch is developed mainly by another Internet giant Facebook, specifically the Facebook API research lab. As with all deep learning libraries PyTorch is supported by GPUs acceleration and has automatic differentiation so there's no need in this course to use tools like calculus and linear algebra to derive back propagation. If you hate math then you should feel very lucky. In fact we won't discuss back propagation at all despite the fact that it's really the main ingredient that makes everything work. This combined with the fact that a lot of the basic building blocks are already built for you are some of the major advantages which are going to allow us to blast through each section very quickly. In the past it was necessary to focus on each architecture one at a time with RNN being the most complex to implement these days ANN, CNN and RNNs can be implemented in just a few lines of code. All right so how is this code structured. First before we even begin discussing deep learning or any type of statistical modeling we are going to look at a new coding environment which I really like called Google Colab. Google Colab is basically Jupyter notebook hosted by Google but with a lot more bells and whistles. Personally I have never been a fan of Jupyter notebook since it seemed to have more disadvantages than advantages. However Google Colab is a different beast. It's hosted by Google so you don't have to use your own computing resources. It's free so it doesn't matter if you have a slow computer or a fast computer. Everyone has the same access it gives you free access to the GPUs and TPUs. You for orders of magnitude faster training and inference and finally most of what we need is already installed so you don't have to waste any time installing libraries yourself. Once you've done that we are going to go through the fundamental architectures involved in deep learning. Believe it or not this all starts with linear regression the line of best fit you learned about in high school physics. We'll see that with just one little change adding the logistic function on top of a linear model. We will get a neuron this covers the two major types of supervised learning classification and regression. Once you know the basics it's time to get started with deep learning. The first deep learning architecture you'll learn about is the artificial neural network also known these days as the deep neural network. Although neither of these names really do a good job of differentiating it with other architectures. Next we'll dive into image processing with convolution on their own that works. You'll learn about convolution and how this works to create neural networks that are specially designed to achieve better performance on images and other physical signals next you'll learn about recurrent neural networks which specialize at working with sequence data. Unlike my previous courses where we used RNNs is mostly for natural language processing we are going to start with time series forecasting. This is going to let us cover a lot of ground that many other courses simply skip over entirely in particular. We're going to cover the difference between the wrong way to do a time series forecast and the right way we're going to look at several time series that simple models like linear regression can and can't solve as well as several time series that slightly more complex models like the simple are in can and can't solve for the more difficult problems we'll see how the LSTM achieves superior performance and so you'll see first hand why LSTM are useful rather than me just telling you and you accepting it as fact without observing it for yourself. The next example is one of my favorites in the chorus which is on stock prediction with LSTMs and RNNs. I think most of you will find the contents of these lectures very surprising. If you've ever learned about stock prediction with Ellis teams in the past be warned most other instructors are doing this the wrong way. In this course I'm going to teach you why it's wrong how to correct it and what some of the real obstacles are in stock prediction. The first major part of this course is about the fundamental architectures and deep learning while the second major part of this course is focused on applications. As a side note if you want to just skip the rest of this lecture and move on with the rest of the course that's fine too. The first application we will look at is natural language processing. Specifically with text documents you'll see how we can use deep learning for text classification which is the type of task you would use for spam detection sentiment analysis and so on. We'll also look at embedding which are deep learnings method of dealing with categorical data embedding will lead us to our next application on recommender systems. Now it might seem weird to think that natural language processing would be somehow related to recommender systems but hopefully in this course you will learn about the hidden connection between these two different fields recommender systems is all about how to optimize the products or items that you recommend to your users. Facebook Amazon and Google have been using recommender systems to improve their profits by the billions. When you go to Amazon.com it is full of recommended products for you. Facebook news feed and your Instagram feed are both recommendation lists. Google's search results advertisements and the YouTube sidebar are all examples of how Google uses recommendations. In short, recommender systems are one of the most practical business applications of deep learning and one that can be used in a pretty straightforward manner to improve your profits. This is in contrast to say natural language where it's not exactly clear how that would directly tie in to how much money your business makes. Although it's already a fundamental part of our day to day lives. So don't discount it just yet. The next application we'll discuss was a game changer for deep learning. If you've taken any of my deep learning courses in the past you know that training a deep neural network takes time lots of time. You might end up waiting hours or even days or possibly even weeks. Luckily machine learning engineers have found new ways of allowing us to build on top of the work of others. The idea is companies like Google or Facebook or university research groups will train large neural networks on humongous datasets such as ImageNet which contains over a million images. That's not the kind of thing you can feasibly do on your home computer using transfer learning what we can do is take just a part of their neural network and combine it with our own neural network designed for a specific task that we want to do. Results have shown that this is an easy. And more importantly fast method of building state of the art deep learning models. In just a few seconds you can integrate the power of bleeding edge networks that works into your own applications. Next we have GANs or generative adversarial networks. This was named as the most interesting invention in machine learning in the past 10 years. By Yann LeCun -- a deep learning pioneer who is now the chief A.I. Scientist at Facebook. GANs are all about generating images using a system of two neural networks one that generates the images and one whose job it is to discriminate between a real and fake images. Using this pair of neural networks they both help each other improve so the discriminator becomes better and better at recognizing fakes. While the generator becomes better and better at creating realistic images that cannot be differentiated from fakes when people think about deep learning they don't often think about how neural network can be used to generate things but rather just how neural networks can make predictions on things. Predictions are nice but generating things opens up a whole new world. Recently Google announced a conversational A.I. Where you could have a personal assistant do something like call a restaurant and make a reservation for you. But that personal assistant is not a person. It is a robot. All of its speech is generated by a computer another exciting application of deep learning is in a reinforcement learning usually deep learning is used to create models with a static input and output. For example you put in an image and it tells you what this image is of like a car or a truck or you put in an email and you're known that work tells you if it's spam or not spam. But some tasks require multiple steps which requires having some long term strategy and keeping track of state. For example if you are playing a game like Super Mario you can't just look at a still image of the game and decide what to do. Instead you need to have a long term strategy. You have to know that you should walk forward to reach the flag for that level. You have to know that if an enemy is walking towards you you have to avoid it or attack it. And also you have to have proper timing in doing so. This is what reinforcement learning is all about. To summarize the outline of the Course is like this. We can split it into two parts Part 1 architectures and part 2 applications. In part one we discuss the fundamental architectures such as linear models, ANNs, CNNs, RNNs. In part two, we discuss applications such as NLP, recommender systems, GANs, transfer learning, reinforcement learning and possibly more. Thanks for listening and I'll see you in the next lecture.

Think of something simple like exercise. If I do 20 pushups Well I gain twice as much muscle as I would have if I did 10 pushups. If I do 30 pushups will I gain three times as much muscle. Of course the answer is No. Otherwise we'd have people doing push ups all the time and becoming very large people. At some point the benefit of doing push ups is going to taper off. Now let's turn our attention to another kind of machine learning problem known as classification both classification and regression are examples of supervised learning which is going to be the main focus of this course we will sometimes discuss unsupervised learning as well but the main focus will be supervised learning so whereas regression is concerned with predicting a real value. No classification is concerned with predicting a category one popular example is image classification where your model accepts as input an image of a dog or a cat and tries to predict whether the label should be dog or cat. However in this lecture we are going to look at an example that helps us build this geometrical intuition we've been talking about so let's say I want to predict the risk of cardiovascular disease given a patient's height and weight. This is a categorical problem because my prediction is either going to be at risk or not at risk. Again this comes down to a data collection experiment. I'm going to look at all my hospital records and I'm going to write down all of this information in an Excel spreadsheet. I'll have two columns to represent my X and one column to represent my target y by the way. Note that it's customary to represent binary targets as the integers 0 and 1. So he would say not at risk is zero and at risk is 1. Note that there is no reason that at risk should be one. Just like the dogs and cats example it doesn't matter of dogs or one and cats are zero or dogs or zero and cats are one. This assignment is just arbitrary OK. So now that I've collected all my data what am I going to do. Well again I'm going to apply these on a grid on the horizontal axis. I'm going to have my first feature the patient's height on the vertical axis. I'm going to have my second feature the patient's weight now importantly unlike regression. The target does not get its own axis instead because it's categorical we would represent it with color so I might color the at risk patients as blue and then not at risk patients as green. So what is my model going to be for classification. Well the simplest model again is a line. However this line is a little bit different from our regression line from earlier. The regression line if you would call was the line of best fit. We are trying to get the line to be close to all the data points. Now we are no longer trying to do that. Instead we are trying to get the line to separate the two groups of data points or in other words separate the different colors as you can see this again boils down to a geometry problem. How do we find this line that can indeed separate these categories one lesson that goes hand-in-hand with the geometrical perspective is another motto of mine. All data is the same. Let's use another example to illustrate the point suppose instead of working at a hospital you now work and an insurance company your job is to do fraud detection or in other words classify instances of fraud. So again you have two categories fraud or not fraud you're trying to predict whether or not a given claim is fraud. Let's say again you've collected some data points. Again with two input features. Suppose these are number one the amount of debt the claimant has. And number two the total amount of past insurance claims and again it's the same story. Once you've collected all your data points you're going to plot them and color them on a grid your job again is to separate these data points with a line or a curve. So you see that just because we change the meaning of the problem we haven't changed what our actual task is. It's still to plot these points and separate them with some kind of decision boundary a line is the simplest. But just like with regression there are two ways we can make this more complicated. The first way is that we can have more input features so that it's not possible to plot them on a grid that we can visualize. The second way is that the decision boundary may not be linear in which case the model will be an equation that's more complicated than a line or hyperplane. Importantly however the moral of the story remains the same. This is still a geometry problem and in fact for our two classification examples the geometry problem was the same. The only thing that changed was the meaning of the numbers of course machine learning algorithms don't care about these meanings and so they are essentially irrelevant in the eyes of the machine learning model. That's why we say all data is the same. This becomes a very powerful concept in the future. For example the same kind of model used for neural machine translation can also be used for a chatbot. The same kind of model used for sentiment analysis can also be used for spam detection in thinking in this way essentially gives you machine learning superpowers. To summarize this lecture the goal was to take the magic away from machine learning you learned a very important lesson which is that machine learning is a magic. In fact it's just geometry. We learned about the two different kinds of geometry problems that supervised learning can solve. The first kind is regression where we try to get a line a plane a hyperplane or curve to be as close as possible to the data points from a given dataset. The second kind is classification where instead of trying to get the curve as close as possible to the data points we try to separate data points belonging to different categories one important lesson that goes along with this is that all data is the same. It doesn't matter if we're trying to classify risk of cardiovascular disease or if we're trying to classify fraud in an insurance company. The general problem remains the same and it is a problem of geometry.

But it was also the most important. Now you see why. So as you recall, we need to define a loss function. Then after we've done that, all we need to do is apply the gradient descent procedure to update the parameters of the model in order to minimize that loss. Once we've completed training, we can plot the loss per iteration to ensure that the loss converges successfully, and we can test our model by checking its accuracy on the train and test sets. The main difference in the training process between regression and classification is that we have a different loss function. As you recall, in regression our target is a real number and our prediction is also a real number. In this scenario, it makes sense to use a loss like the mean squared error or MSE. But in classification our target is a category. Our model output is the probability that the input belongs to each of the categories. So the mean squared error doesn't make any sense in this scenario. In fact, for classification, what we want is the cross entropy loss. There's one little wrinkle here, which is that we're doing binary classification in which there are only two possible classes, and the corresponding loss is called the binary cross entropy loss. In general, if your model can handle any number of classes, then you'll use the regular cross entropy loss. But we'll discuss that later in this course. The reasoning behind the cross entropy loss is quite a bit more complicated than the mean squared error, so we won't discuss that theory in this lecture. As you saw, it was very similar to linear regression in the sense that our model is still a line or a hyperplane, but it's how we use this line that's different in regression. Our goal is to get the line close to the data points, but in classification, our goal is to separate the data points. In regression, we just pass our data into W times X plus B and that is our prediction. But in classification we still pass our data through W, times X plus B, we just have the additional steps of applying the sigmoid function and rounding the output probability for number three. But the difference in classification is that instead of using the mean squared error, we use the cross entropy. And in our special case of binary classification, we use the binary cross entropy.

In this lecture we are going to look at the models we just used more in depth. Specifically if you know a little bit about machine learning you may recognize that the models we just used are called linear regression and logistic regression. We use logistic regression for classification and we use linear regression for regression. So this lecture will look at how these models work and also explain why we refer to logistic regression as a neuron. Just to remind you of the high level picture here. Deep Learning is the study of neural networks and neural networks are networks of neurons. So you can think of these as the basic fundamental unit of computation in deep learning let's start with linear regression in its most basic form linear regression just means line of best fit. As you may recall from your high school math studies a line has the equation y hat equals M X plus b here X is the input variable M is the slope and B is the y intercept. When we put these together we get the equation for a line our job of course is to find a line that best fits our input data to give you a simple example of how we would use linear regression. Let's suppose we are trying to predict your salary based on how many years of experience you have. So in this case x would be the number of years of experience and y would be your salary. Now you might be wondering what is the interpretation of the slope in y intercept. In this scenario. Well let's try to play around with this equation a little bit and see what happens. We know that b the y intercept is the value of y half when x equals zero. So in other words if you have zero years of experience this would be your salary. B If X equals 1 that means you have one year of experience and then your salary would be M Plus B if x equals two. That means you have two years of experience and then your salary would be two M plus B. In other words M is the increase in salary that you get for each additional year of experience. Of course in the real world we might want to make a prediction about your salary based on multiple factors instead of just years of experience. We might have another input let's say average industry salary. So now your salary can also depend on what industry you are working in. So we'll call it years of experience x 1 and we'll call average industry salary x 2 in this scenario. We would write out our model as Y equals w 1 x 1 plus W2 x 2 plus B in this equation w 1 and W2 are called the weights of the model and they are essentially the slope for each of the individual inputs X1 and X2 luckily the interpretation is the same as what we saw previously. W 1 is the increase in salary when X1 increases by 1 W2 is the increase in salary when x 2 increases by 1. B is the salary when both X1 and x 2 or 0 another way to think of the weights is that they tell us how important each input is to predicting the output. Imagine the extreme scenario where we have some w sub i equals zero. In this case it doesn't matter how much we increase or decrease x sub i the output will not change at all. So in other words x sub i has no influence on the output. That's another way of saying x sub i is irrelevant. Now imagine that w sub i is very large in magnitude. Note that it can be either very positive or very negative. This means that x sub i has a large influence on the output. Because a small increase in x sub i leads to a large increase in output that's just another way of saying that this input feature is very important. Also the sign of w sub i controls the direction of the influence. If w sub i is very positive then an increase in x sub i will lead to a large increase in the output. If w sub i is very negative then an increase in x sub i will lead to a large decrease in the output now in what way is any of this related to neurons. Well to understand this you have to understand a little bit about biology. A neuron is a cell in your brain. You can think of it as we said before as the fundamental unit of computation neurons can talk to other neurons using electrical and chemical signals. So if you picture a neuron you can imagine that there are many other incoming neurons attached to it. These input terminals are called dendrites. As you can see in this image those incoming neurons might come from say your eyes or your ears or your nose or your hands. So if your eyes see something an electrical signal goes along the nerves in your eyes and travels to your brain the same thing happens when you hear something or you smell something or you touch something. Now remember we're picturing a single neuron it's taking in inputs from a lot of different places. Now this neuron it has to decide if it's going to pass this signal on to outgoing neurons because remember this neurons kind of in the middle there are some neurons going into it and it's going out to some other neurons. Now how does it do that. Well it does that in a very similar way to linear and logistic regression. It sums up all the incoming signals and then this summation becomes the outgoing signal that gets passed on further down the chain. The next thing you have to know is that not all neuron connections are created equal. Some connections are strong while others are weak. Some connections excite the receiving neuron while other connections inhibit the receiving neuron. This is just like the weights of a regression model. A large weight either positive or negative has a strong influence on the output. That's a strong connection. A small or nearly zero weight has only a weak influence on the output so that's a weak connection. A positive weight influences the output in the positive direction. So that's like an excitatory neuron and a negative weight influences the output in the negative direction. So that's like an inhibitory neuron the signal that gets passed along neurons has a special name. It's called an action potential. Basically it's a spike in electrical potential. So if you measure the electrical potential over time at a particular point in the neuron you would see a signal like this. Now action potentials don't behave in a very intuitive way. In particular you can think of them as binary outcomes just like logistic regression. In other words the neuron is more like logistic regression than linear regression although the linear regression equation is the main calculation that takes place in both cases. So here's how the action potential works. Basically we're going to sum up all the influences from all the incoming neurons. If the electrical potential of this sum is greater than some threshold then an action potential will propagate through the receiving neuron if the electrical potential is less than this threshold then nothing happens at all. This is very much like binary classification where we make predictions which are either 0 or 1 in biology. We call this the all or nothing principle either an action potential fires or doesn't. As you can see here when the stimulus is too weak there's only a little bump in the response. So those are not action potentials but once the stimulus reaches a certain threshold a full action potential spike occurs. So there's no such thing as a spectrum of action potentials like an action potential of one volt two volts three volts and so forth. Instead it's just a binary decision. You get a spike or you don't. The incoming signals summed together are strong enough to generate the next action potential or they will simply be ignored so that's how you can think of logistic regression as a neuron. Each x sub i is an input from some incoming neuron. Each w sub i is a weight that tells us how strong the connection with x sub i is and the sign of w sub i tells us whether that connection is excitatory meaning it positively influences an action potential or inhibitory meaning it negatively influences an action potential. The weighted sum of each x sub i which is then added to the bias term or threshold is then passed to the sigmoid function. Once the sigmoid function is rounded we get either 1 or 0 telling us whether or not an action potential should occur.

In this lecture we are going to answer the question how does a model learn. Let's start with linear regression and its most basic form linear regression just means line of best fit. As you may recall from your high school math studies a line has the equation y equals M X plus b here X is the input variable M is the slope and B is the y intercept. When we put these together we get the equation for a line and our job of course is to find a line that best fits our input data so you can imagine that our input data is a bunch of data points that approximately create the shape of a line. This plot is called a scatter plot. So for each point x and y in our dataset we're going to draw a dot on this chart. Our goal is to find the line that best passes through all these data points. In practice this means finding the slope and y intercept one method. You may have used in high school is to take a ruler and to try and draw the best line on paper using visual inspection. Of course since this is data science we no longer use such methods. We have to be more systematic. The line that you draw might not be the same as the line that I draw. And furthermore if we are in multiple dimensions this won't be a line at all. So it's clear that we need something better and more quantitative. The idea is we're going to define an error function for each data point which is a pair made up of the input x i and the target y. We're going to calculate a prediction y hat i equals m x i plus B then we are going to take the squared difference between y i and y hat i we're going to do this for each of our data points for I equals one up to n once we've done this we can add them all up and divide by n. This is called the mean squared error. It's the average squared deviation between our predictions and our targets. Basically this is going to tell us how accurate our model is. If you think about what we just looked at neural networks for binary classification and neural networks for regression they are not that different from what we looked at previously. If we look at just the final layers they look just like regular old linear regression and logistic regression. That's what we studied in the previous section. So here's a new way to think about neural networks instead of merely a network of layers of neurons. Really we're just doing a series of feature transformations so we go from feature to feature to feature. And then finally we just have a plain linear regression for regression or logistic regression for classification using these uniform layers. Researchers noticed that neural networks were able to learn hierarchies of features each layer seemed to be learning something more complex than the last. And this was the motivation for making neural networks deep. And that's why this field is called deep learning one of my favorite examples of this is with facial recognition networks by visualizing what each layer has learned. Researchers found that the initial layers just learned some basic lines and strokes and in the middle the neural network started to learn about specific features of faces such as eyes nose mouth and so on. Finally at the final layers the neural networks started to see entire faces. In other words neural networks are able to break down a problem into smaller sub problems or in other words a hierarchy.

In this lecture we are going to discuss activation functions. Previously we learned that the sigmoid function allows us to build neural networks and it does several important things for us. First it maps its inputs to go from zero to 1. This is nice because it mimics the biological neuron. So our neural network is literally a network of artificial neurons. Second and this is more practical. It makes our neural network nonlinear. The function itself is non-linear and it also makes it so that we can't reduce the neural network into a simple linear equation. At the same time in modern Deep Learning we've discovered that there are some problems with the sigmoid. And so it is no longer used as often except in some specific cases if you recall something we discussed earlier was the importance of standardization. We don't want to have one input in the range one million to 5 million and then another input going from zero to zero point 0 0 0 1 instead we would like to have all of our data centered around zero and in approximately the same range. Now the sigmoid is problematic in this regard. If you recall the output of a sigmoid is always between 0 and 1 and its middle value is therefore zero point five. Therefore the output of a sigmoid can never be centered around zero. This goes back to our idea of the uniformity of a neural network one layer of a neural network takes as input the output of the previous layer. So if the previous layer is outputting numbers centered around zero point five that's not quite right. This is because this output is going to become the input to the next layer and the next layer wants to also see inputs which are standardized. Therefore we want both the inputs and the output of each layer to be standardized luckily there is a solution to this although it takes away from this idea that a neuron network is made up of this idealized neuron simulation instead of using the sigmoid we'll use a function that has the exact same shape as the sigmoid just centered around zero. This function is called the tanh which is short for hyperbolic tangent if you recall there are hyperbolic versions of all the trigonometric functions. So there is a hyperbolic sine hyperbolic cosine and so forth. Well it turns out that the hyperbolic tangent analogously to the trigonometric tangent is just the hyperbolic sine over the hyperbolic cosine and it has the equation you see here the sigmoid has a similar equation one divided by one plus the exponent of minus X. The major difference between the sigmoid and the tanh is that the sigmoid goes between 0 and 1 while the tanh goes between minus 1 and plus 1 as an exercise. You may want to try and prove the relationship between the sigmoid and the tanh in particular that the tanh is just a scaled and vertically shifted version of the sigmoid now although the tanh is a little better than the sigmoid the story is not over in modern deep learning. Researchers have figured out that there is actually a problem with both of these activation functions. I like to tell this story as a bit of a cautionary tale for a long time. Researchers were very attached to the beauty of neural networks as is they liked this idea of a uniform neural network made up of idealized neurons. They like this idea that the sigmoid and hence also the tanh were smooth differentiable functions. It is mathematically convenient and beautiful. The problem is they don't work that well but nobody wanted to break away from this classic way of doing things the major problem with sigmoid and tanh is called the vanishing gradient problem. Now this part requires a little bit of calculus knowledge. So if you're not comfortable with that then feel free to skip ahead. Remember that our method of training a neural network is gradient descent. And obviously this involves finding the gradient of the cost with respect to the parameters. The problem is when you have a very deep neural network your gradient has to propagate backwards throughout the neural network starting from the end. What happens is your output is made up of a bunch of composite functions basically a sigmoid of a sigmoid of a sigmoid and so on when you take the gradient of composite functions you get the chain rule so composite functions become multiplication in the derivative. So what does this end up looking like. Well the further you go back in the neural network the more terms you have in the chain rule to multiply. So you're multiplying by the derivative of the sigmoid. Over and over again what happens when you do that. Why is the derivative of the sigmoid a problem well consider what the sigmoid actually looks like most of the sigmoid is flat. In other words the derivative of the sigmoid is very nearly zero at most points only in the center is it non-zero. It also turns out that the maximum value of the derivative is only zero point two five. This is the highest possible value of the derivative of the sigmoid. Okay so why is that a problem. Well what happens when you multiply numbers that are very small. The answer is you get an even smaller number. Let's say you multiply zero point two five. The maximum possible value five times the result is zero point two five to the power five which is approximately zero point zero zero one. What happens if more realistically you have a value like zero point one multiplied by itself five times. That's zero point one to the power five which is zero point zero zero zero zero one. In other words this leads the result that the further you go back in the neural network the smaller the gradient becomes. We call this the vanishing gradient problem. So how does this problem manifest. We'll take a look at this graph which shows the magnitude of the gradient at each layer of the neural network as it is trained. You'll notice that the further you go back the smaller the gradient gets. Remember that the training algorithm is to take small steps in the direction of the gradient. Well if the gradient is nearly zero that means the update to the weights is also nearly zero. The end result is that weights close to the input of the neural network are almost not trained at all. This was a problem in the olden days which prevented us from building very deep neural networks like we have today which can have hundreds of layers back in the day. There was lots of theory around how to solve this problem. One method was called a greedy layer wise pre training which was invented by Geoffrey Hinton and his students. Since all the layers of the neural network could not be trained all at once the idea was you could train each layer one at a time so what you would do is train the first layer using some alternative loss function. By the way if you want to know what that loss function is it's basically an autoencoder but hold that thought for now as it's not an important detail then once you were done training the first layer you would add on a second layer and train that layer by itself not touching the first layer anymore. Then you would add a third layer and train only the third layer leaving the first two layers alone. Once you got to the last layer all of the previous layers would already be trained to some extent. Now despite all this theory which generated lots of theoretical research into new models such as restricted boltzmann machines deep Boltzmann machines and so forth today we no longer require such complicated models in order to train very deep neural networks although that's not to say they're not worth learning about. In fact the solution was simple Just don't use activation functions that have vanishing gradients. So throw away these beautiful smooth differential functions like the tanh and the sigmoid instead. Let's use this ugly looking not completely differentiable function called the ReLU the ReLU is short for rectified linear unit. Basically it looks like a hockey stick and it has a corner at zero where the derivative is technically not defined. The fact that values greater than zero never have a zero gradient makes training neural networks a lot more efficient. Now you might be wondering wait a minute. If a zero gradients are so bad then why does the ReLU work at all. It appears that half the function any input less than zero has a derivative that is exactly zero. Never mind vanishing the gradient is already vanished. Indeed this is somewhat of a problem as it leads to a phenomenon called Dead neurons. The neurons are neurons that always output zero because the weighted sum of its inputs are always less than or equal to zero. However and this is important in deep learning what we care about is experimental results. In other words the most important thing is that it works not how theoretically satisfying is because as we now know that can lead to lots of wasted time. The fact that just the right side doesn't vanish seems to be good enough according to what we've observed. Of course some researchers have tried to make modifications to the simple ReLU to solve this problem of dead neurons. One alternative is the leaky ReLU which has a slope of less than one like zero point one for values less than zero. Importantly this is still a nonlinear function so we're able to learn non-linear geometrical patterns using the leaky ReLU your derivatives will always be positive. Just like the sigmoid and the tanh there are other options as well such as the ELU or exponential linear unit which has a more steadily decreasing value on the left side. The authors claim that this activation function speeds up learning and leads to higher accuracy than the ReLU. One interesting aspect of the ELU is that it allows its outputs to be negative which goes back to the idea that we like the mean of the values to be close to zero another option which is very similar is the softplus activation which because you're taking the log of the exponent looks very linear when the input is reasonably large now for both of these previous activation functions. There is the vanishing gradient on the left side but we've established that it's not so much of a problem since we know that the ReLU already works and it has gradients that are equal to zero also. Although we initially stated that we would like the inputs at each layer to be centered around zero we can see that the ReLU and softplus do not accomplish this for the softplus and the ReLU the minimum value is zero while the maximum value is infinity. This definitely means they won't be centered around zero. So is the ReLU not a good choice in the end. Now despite all this work to find alternatives to the ReLU activation these days most people still use the ReLU as a reasonable default choice. It works well and sometimes you'll find that using other alternatives such as the leaky ReLU or the ELU offer no benefit. Sometimes they do. Which is why you always have to experiment for yourself. My motto which a lot of my students are tired of hearing by this point is that machine learning is experimentation and not philosophy. Never use your mind to try and predict the outcome of a computer program. If you have a computer that is always the suboptimal course of action why not simply run the computer program with a computer. Your mind is not suitable for running computer programs but computers are therefore follow the rule. Don't use philosophy use experimentation interestingly some researchers have talked about the biological plausibility of the ReLU activation function. In fact it may even be more biologically plausible than the sigmoid to understand this you have to understand a little more about how action potentials encode information. What is the difference between an action potential. When you hear a quiet sound versus an action potential. When you hear a loud sound. The answer is there is no difference. An action potential is just an action potential. The key really is in the frequency of action potentials. When you hear a very quiet sound your neurons are only activated a little bit so you'll get some action potentials but they won't be very frequent. If you hear a very loud sound like say you're at a concert or a party then your neurons are getting lots of stimulation. The action potentials are going to be very frequent. In other words closer together in time. So what we're saying is the more intense a stimulus is the higher the frequency of the action potentials. We call this frequency coding what does this mean in terms of the ReLU. Well you can think of it as the ReLU is just encoding the actual potential frequency itself. Of course the minimum frequency is zero and it's not possible to have a negative frequency. That's why the minimum value of the ReLU is zero. Then as the inputs into the neuron get larger because they are being stimulated more the receiving neuron also gets stimulated more increasing its frequency now. One thing to note is that we can go even deeper than this although this is not part of mainstream deep learning quite yet. As a side note if you don't want to listen to this part it's not required. It's something that I think is interesting to those of us who are interested in modelling brains. But if you are a hardcore statistician then perhaps you may think differently what we know based on neuroscience is that unlike the ReLU activation action potential frequency is not linearly related to its input stimuli. Instead we have a nonlinear relationship. It can be modeled using the log function or a root function like the square root a good way to understand this is with sound something that is twice as loud does not sound twice as loud. Using measurements of sound intensity this is the intuition behind the decibel scale. As you recall the decibel scale is a logarithmic scale. For example a 90 decibels sound would be like sitting inside a moving bus 100 decibels sound would be like standing by an electric saw at 110 decibels sound would be like a loud orchestra of 120 decibels sound would be like standing near a jet engine. A 130 decibels sound would be like being close to artillery fire and this value is the threshold of pain. So when you hear a sound this loud it actually hurts physically. To put that in perspective 100 decibels is ten times more powerful than 90 decibels 110 decibels is 100 times more powerful 120 decibels is 1000 times more powerful and 130 decibels is ten thousand times more powerful some work has been done to experiment with activation functions that more accurately model the frequency characteristics of real neurons such as the bee are you. But as a whole they haven't yet caught on in the Deep Learning Community. I've attached the paper on the bee are you to extra reading dot txt in case you want to check it out. The author reports that the BYU activation function led to better results than the ReLU and the ELU. So it may be something worth trying in your own project.

In this lecture we are going to discuss another very important topic multi class classification previously we discuss the binary classification which used a sigmoid at the output. We also had sigmoid for the hidden layer activation functions but we just got rid of that in favor of the ReLU which tends to work better for the output. However if we are doing binary classification the sigmoid is still the right choice binary classification has many applications. We can predict disease or notices is the user fraudulent or not. Well the user click my ad or not. Will the user accept a friend request or not. And so on and so forth. But there are situations that binary classification cannot handle such as when we might have multiple categorical outcomes let's think of some examples. One example is optical character recognition or handwriting recognition. If we want to recognize alphanumeric characters then there are at least 36 possibilities 10 digits and 26 letters. What about speech recognition. If we want to recognize words then each word counts as a separate category image classification is another one and for a long time this was the standard benchmark which proved that deep learning works better than other machine learning models. You may have heard of a famous dataset called the ImageNet dataset which is made up of millions of images in the thousand categories such as bagel vending machine and soccer ball. Every year there is a contest to see who can build the best ImageNet classifier and of course these are all deep learning models. So how does multi class classification work. Well suppose we have just calculated the activation at the final layer of our neural network but have not yet applied the activation function. So we have a superscript l equal to w superscript l transpose dot z superscript l minus 1. So that's the Z at the previous layer plus b superscript l it's important to remember that if the layer size is k then a superscript l is a vector of size k what we would like to do is map these values to probabilities for each of the K possible output categories. Okay so that's your first lesson here. If we have K possible outcomes then we should have K output nodes. The question now is what function can actually map the vector a superscript l 2 probability values let's think about what the requirements are for these probabilities. We need a probability distribution over a K distinct values. As a side note we assign these values the integers 0 to K minus 1 first since they are probabilities. They must be non negative. In other words they must be greater than or equal to zero. But there is also an upper limit. The maximum value of a probability is 1. But more importantly for this to be a proper probability distribution all the possible different values must sum to 1. So the second requirement is that all the probabilities must sum to 1 luckily there is a function that accomplishes exactly this. It is called the softmax function first let's drop the superscript l on the activation a for now so we can just say a is a vector of size k then the softmax of this vector A is the exponential of a divided by the sum of the exponential of a across each component. As you can see this satisfies both of our requirements. The exponential of any number is always positive so therefore each probability must be non negative. Second because the denominator is just the sum of all the possible values of the numerator. Then if we sum all the possible values of the numerator we just get the same sum and therefore we get the same sum on the top and the bottom and they cancel out to give us 1 now that we know how the softmax works. Let's answer the most important question how do we use it in PyTorch. Well just like most other functions we've applied so far it's very simple. There is an object we instantiate called softmax. In other words the only requirement is that you spell it correctly. Of course you can always implement the softmax yourself but in PyTorch there's no need. As a side note the softmax is considered an activation function but unlike the ReLU sigmoid and tanh it is not meant for a hidden layer activations if you want to try using the softmax as a hidden layer activation you are most welcome to but you'll generally find that it doesn't work that well. So the softmax is technically an activation function but we normally only use it when we're trying to get an output probability from a vector of activation values such as at the end of a neural network now that you know how to use the softmax in PyTorch. The next thing I'm going to tell you is to not use it just like we learned earlier with the sigmoid and the binary cross entropy PyTorch combines those two functions into a single loss for numerical stability. So PyTorch is going to combine the softmax function with the cross entropy loss into this single loss which is simply called cross entropy loss PyTorch does in fact have a standalone categorical loss which is called NLL loss but that is outside the scope of this course. In the example below we've implemented logistic regression but instead of being a binary logistic regression it's now a multi class logistic regression that predicts k different categories. As you can see the model is still just a basic linear layer. All the magic really happens inside the cross entropy loss object. The last thing I want to do in this lecture is summarize the three types of tasks we've encountered so far that neural nets can perform and their corresponding activation functions two of them you already saw in the previous section of this course. And now we have a third. So first we have a regression where we use it no activation function at all. Sometimes we also call this the identity function which is just a fancy way of saying a function that returns its input. Second we have binary classification where we use the sigmoid activation function using the sigmoid. We only need one output node because since we know the probability of the output being one the probability of the output being 0 is just 1 minus that. This is the same type of thing you see when you're looking at the Bernoulli distribution versus the categorical distribution the Bernoulli distribution is a categorical distribution where there can only be two outcomes. Thus it only has one parameter. The categorical distribution on the other hand if it has K outcomes it also has K parameters. And that brings us to our third scenario which is multi class classification. For this we use the softmax activation function one important thing to mention that sometimes confuses people is that these three activation functions apply whether you are using a feed forward neural network a linear model or even a more complicated network like a CNN or an RNN. It doesn't matter what kind of model you have these three activation functions always correspond to these three tasks. So for example if I don't want to use a neural network but just a simple linear classifier for multiple classes then I would have just a single dense layer with a softmax activation. This is still called logistic regression by the way. It's just not binary logistic regression. Instead it's called multi class logistic regression it's important to remember that what came before the final layer in the model is not related to the task. You can have a CNN or an RNN or any other kind of complicated neural network. It is still the case that the final layer of the network will be a dense layer with one of these three activation functions corresponding to the task being done. Another important thing to remember is that the softmax function is more general whereas the sigmoid can only handle binary classification. The softmax function can handle multi class classification which includes binary classification. So it's possible if you want to just use the softmax for all types of classification. If you set k equals 2 then you're doing binary classification. It's just that in this scenario your outputs are a bit redundant because you already know that they both sum to one and hence only one of them is really needed.

Only at the same time do we not expect that the sample represents the true population. The answer is usually yes. Do we expect that our measurements on the sample will be close to the measurements we could theoretically take on the entire population? The answer is yes. The same thing happens when we do batch gradient descent, even though we are only looking at a small sample of the data at any given time. We do expect that the loss and its gradient will be representative of the entire dataset, which itself is what we expect to be representative of the true distribution of where the data set comes from. Furthermore, on each epoch we still see every data point, so we don't miss anything unlike real world population samples. In other words, a softer version of the max. In other words, the maximum value before we do the softmax will still be the maximum value after we do the softmax. It's just that the softmax happens to map those values to probabilities. Therefore, we just need to pick which of the K outputs has the maximum value and not worry about them being probabilities or not. In PyTorch, this is accomplished with torch dot max, which returns both the maximum value and its index. Finally if the two vectors are orthogonal or at right angles then the dot product should be zero. The reason why this is important is you don't have to think of a filter as an abstract concept. In fact it's just a pattern finder. This actually makes the term filter make a lot more sense. It filters out everything not related to the pattern contained in the filter by setting them to zero and keeps everything that is related to the pattern. So what convolution is doing is it's passing this filter along each point on the original input image and sliding it along at each point. It asks is the pattern here is the pattern here is the pattern here. And so forth. Then it gives us a high number in the positions where the pattern is found and then a small number where the pattern is not found and thus this is your first alternative perspective on convolution. It's just a sliding pattern finder that passes through an entire image. Looking for a particular pattern.

It's saying we don't care what those skipped pixels are because they probably are very close to the pixels we were already looking at. So to summarize the convolution part of our convolutional neural network now looks like this. We can have a series of strided convolutions all with approximately the same filter size with increasing feature maps at each layer. Or we can have a series of convolutions followed by pooling again all with approximately the same filter size and with increasing numbers of feature maps at each layer the last part of this lecture will focus on the second half of the CNN which is the feedforward neural network part. Now there's not much to discuss here except that we have to consider the shape of an image is not appropriate for a dense feedforward network. Remember that when an image comes out of a convolution it's going to be three dimensional height by width by number of feature maps but a feedforward neural network takes in a feature vector a one dimensional object. Luckily we've already discussed how this works. We can turn a 3D object into a one-D object using the view function in PyTorch one alternative to the flatten layer which I really like is the global Max pooling layer. This is a little different from the regular kind of pooling we discussed earlier consider the question. What if we have different sized images. The largest source of images is the internet. Generally speaking images we find on the Internet are not all the same size so it makes sense to wonder is it possible to build a convolutional neural network that is capable of handling different image sizes. And the answer is yes. Using a global Max pooling layer Let's consider first why a simple flatten layer would not work. Suppose again we have an input image of size 32 by 32 and four convolutions assume again we use convolution and same mode. And we have a stride of two. So after the first convolution We get a 16 by 16. After the second convolution We get an eight by eight. After the third convolution We get a four by four. And after the fourth convolution We get a two by two. But now let's say we have an input image of size 64 by 64. In this case the output after four convolutions would be four by four. Let's say for simplicity's sake the number of output feature maps is one hundred then for the 32 by 32 image. Doing a flatten operation would yield an output of size two by two by one hundred two times two times 100 which is four hundred for a sixty four by sixty four image. Doing a flatten operation would yield an output size four times four times 100 which is sixteen hundred. And of course a feedforward neural network is not capable of handling vectors of different sizes. Now let's consider how global max pooling works. The idea is simple if our input image is h by W. By C then the output is one by one by C or equivalently just a vector of size C. In other words it takes a max over the entire image along the spatial dimensions over each feature map. Since we have C feature maps we end up with what is essentially a one dimensional vector of size C since the 1 dimensions are redundant. This follows the same general idea of pooling where we're saying I don't care where in the image the feature was found just that it was found somewhere. Global max pooling is the extreme of this saying that the feature can be found anywhere in the entire image across the entire height and width since the output is always a vector of size C it does not depend on the size of the image meaning that it allows the network to handle images of any size. As a side note we also have global average pooling which is just the global version of regular average pooling. The only exception to this is if your images are too small in which case you'll just get an error when you try to run your code. For example if your image starts out as a two by two then it's not possible to reduce the dimensions by half four times. You'll notice this happens if you do something like add too many convolutions to your neural network. All right so let's summarize the basic architecture of a modern convolutional neural network where the first stage is a series of stride convolutions or optionally convolution followed by pooling and repeating that pattern in the interface between convolution layers and dense layers. We have a flatten. We also optionally have a global Max pooling that reduces the image to just the max for each feature map. Finally once we flattened our data into a one dimensional vector we have a regular feedforward neural network made up of a series of dense layers as usual and as you learned in the previous section the activation and number of nodes for the final layer depends on the type of task being done. So if you're doing scalar regression then you'll only have one output node with no activation function. If you're doing binary classification you could have one output node with a sigmoid. However for k equals two or more classes you can have K output nodes with a softmax activation.

In this lecture, we are going to start discussing modern RNN units, you may have heard of these already, so I'll just tell you right now what they are. The LSTM and the GRU. LSTM stands for long short term memory and GRU stands for gated recurrent unit. They are both essentially the same thing with the GRU meant to be a more simplified and efficient version of the LSTM. This lecture will discuss why the LSTM and GRU are needed in the first place when the simple RNN seems pretty good already. We'll also look at the underlying equations for the LSTM and GRU and importantly a convenient perspective for looking at them. One mistake a lot of beginners make is that they see a bunch of equations and they get very intimidated. They think, what the heck is this? Just a bunch of equations. What do I do with this? So hopefully this lecture will take you from that lazy beginner's mindset to how a proper machine learning engineer would think about LSTMs and GRUs. First, we need to discuss why we have these fancy new recurrent units in the first place. Why is a simple recurrent unit not good enough to understand this? We have to go back to the vanishing gradient problem. As with our RNN, we can represent the output prediction y hat big T as a function of the inputs x1 x2 all the way up to x T. Once we do this, we can see that it's just a really big composite function. Now, suppose we want to take the derivative with respect to W x h we can see that W x h appears several times in this equation. Now, the actual derivatives themselves and how to find them are not what we have to consider here, but what is important is which derivatives are going to show up? Well, if W x h appears multiplied by X of T, then we are going to have to find the derivative of W x h times X of T at some point in our expression for the gradient of W x h, it should be clear that W x h appears in front of all the x values for every time step. So ultimately all of these single derivatives are going to appear somewhere in our expression for the gradient of our cost with respect to W x h. But another thing that's important to consider is how deeply nested each of these terms is with respect to why hat of Big T, what is clear is that the term involving X1 is the most deeply nested. The term involving X2 is the second most deeply nested and so on. Now, what do we remember about the derivative of composite functions from our theory of ANNs? Well, we know that composite functions turn into multiplication in the gradient. This is due to the chain rule of calculus. Therefore, the more deeply nested you are, the more terms you have to multiply by when you're finding the gradient. In other words, RNNs are particularly vulnerable to the vanishing gradient problem. The farther back in the sequence the input is, the more vulnerable it is to the effects of the vanishing gradient. This is why it's often said that RNNs have problems learning long term dependencies, the RNN simply cannot learn from inputs that are too far back. So how does the vanishing gradient problem manifest in actual machine learning applications, let's suppose we're doing natural language processing and we would like to extract some information about a document. So to give you a concrete example, suppose an AI is reading the Wikipedia page about Albert Einstein. It has read the entire page. Now you ask your AI on what day was Albert Einstein born. Unfortunately, a simple RNN would not be able to answer this, even though this information appears in the article. The problem is it appeared at the beginning of the article. So by the end of the article, the simple RNN has simply forgotten what it had read earlier. Now, you might think, aha, I have a solution to this vanishing gradient problem, it is to use ReLUs. Unfortunately, with RNNs, things are not so simple, of course, you can always try to use ReLUs in your RNNs and verify experimentally what the results are, but in deep learning, we found that the most effective way of dealing with this problem is to use entirely different units, namely the LSTM and the GRU. One interesting historical fact is that the LSTM was created a very long time ago, 1997. This is more than a decade before deep learning was even called deep learning. So this is why I always say to people research, interesting ideas. Don't just go through your career chasing what is popular. By doing that, you were like a hamster running on a spinning wheel, going nowhere. If you're only chasing popular mainstream ideas, you would have never come across this idea of LSTMs. It's more than a decade old part of a field that nobody even cares about. Do what is interesting, not what is popular. Now, the LSTM is an extremely complex unit, the GRU was invented more recently in 2014, but it uses a lot of the same ideas. So I always like to start with the GRU so that you can learn the principles in a simpler setting and then go back to the LSTM. So what is the gated recurrent unit? First, let's start with the basic principle from a simple RNN. We still want to have some hidden state at time t h of t this hidden state will still depend on x of t the current input and h of T minus one, the previous hidden state. The only thing that will change is how h of T is calculated. Now, there's a little bit of a debate on how to present the GRU, is it more useful to look at the equations or is it more useful to look at diagrams? Now, if you are a beginner, you might automatically say pictures, pictures of the best for learning. Unfortunately for you, that's not what we are going to do. A lot of poorly written blogs that I'll copy from each other use these same diagrams as if they were self-explanatory. You look at this picture and all of a sudden, bam, you understand LSTMs and GRUs. Personally, I find this doesn't work for me. I know that other prominent lecturers feel the same way. Of course, if you find these pictures useful, you're welcome to look at them and try to make sense of them. But for me and many others I know, it's actually the equations which are most useful that might seem backwards to a beginner who is very terrified of math, but hopefully you are past that point right now. I promise you that there's nothing here that we haven't seen before. OK, so enough chitchat. Where is the GRU? Well, here are the equations for the GRU to sort of give you some perspective on this. I've also included the equation for a simple recurrent unit so that you can compare the complexity of the two. The simple recurrent unit is essentially just one line. h of T depends on x of t and h of T minus one, the GRU is three lines because we have to calculate three different things. First, we calculate z of T, which is called the update gate vector. Second, we calculate r of t, which is called the reset gate vector. And finally we calculate h of T, which is the hidden state vector, which is, as with the simple recurrent unit, what gets passed on to the next layer in the neural network. So let's analyze these equations so that we can make sense of the GRU. First, it's important to discuss shapes, you want some visualization of the objects we're dealing with? Well, it's helpful to know that all of these new vectors are just vectors of size m the same size as H of T, as always. This is a hyperparameters, so you can choose how many features the hidden layer should have. This also implies the shape of all these weights. If a weight is going from X of T to one of the gate vectors, then it must be of size D by M. If a weight is going from h of T minus one to one of the gate vectors, then it must be of size M by M. And of course, since all the vectors are of size M, then all of the bias terms must also be of size M. Next, let us consider what the GRU is trying to do. I think the names are very helpful here. z of T is the update gate vector and r of T is the reset gate vector. By the way, if you didn't know the circle with a dot in, it means element-wise multiplication. So one minus Z is an M size vector and h of T minus one is also an M size vector. When you multiply these together, you are doing element-wise multiplication. So let us start by looking at z of t how is it used? We can see that z of t gets multiplied by one term involving x of t and h of T minus one, then one minus Z gets multiplied by the previous hidden state, h of T minus one. This is very helpful. You can think of ZT as telling us what should we do? Should we take this new value for the hidden state, or should we just remember the previous hidden state h of T minus one? Why is that helpful? Well, remember what we learned about the vanishing gradient. If we use a simple RNN, it is prone to forgetting things that it has seen in the past by using this gate, it explicitly allows us to remember the previous hidden state so that the hidden state can be carried forward to the next hidden state. By the way, since ZT is the output of a sigmoid, its values are always between a zero and one. Therefore, for h of T, we are always taking a weighted some of the previous H of T minus one and this other function. So if z of t is close to zero, then we will remember the old value h of T minus one. But if it is close to one, then we'll take the new value and forget the old H of T minus one. By the way, you can think of this other function as analogous to what the simple RNN is doing. This is very important, but there's one more piece of the puzzle before we can move on to a helpful interpretation of what's going on. I want you to look very carefully at this equation for z of T, what does this look like to you? Well, it is a sigmoid of some dot products, plus a bias term. What does that look like? Well, you might recognize this as exactly like a dense layer. Now, you might object saying that there are two weights. So it's not exactly like a dense layer. But in fact, the way that these units are often implemented, what we do is we concatenate X of T and H of T minus one into a single vector. Let us just call it V for short. If we concatenate those inputs and we concatenate the weights, then we just get back to our regular old dense layer where we have one input multiplied by one weight matrix plus a bias term. In other words, what is this? This is just a neuron. Now notice that it also ends with a sigmoid. Importantly, this sigmoid is not a hyperparameter. This is usually always a sigmoid because the output is always a number between a zero and one. That's how we can take Z of T and one minus z of T later on in the GRU. So what is this neuron predicting? It's like a binary classifier telling us essentially the probability that we should take the new value for h of T or if we should keep the old value of T minus one. So if we ignore the reset gate for now, here is how we can interpret the GRU first, remember that h of T is essentially the weighted sum of two things, h of T minus one and the output of a simple RNN. Z of T, the update gate vector is like an output probability, telling us the probability that we should keep the output of the simple RNN in other words, keep h of T minus one with probability one minus C of T and keep the simple RNN output with probability z of T. The final h of T is then just a mixture of these two, allowing us to keep the most important parts of h of T minus one and discard the rest. Now, I want to make one small clarification, please note that this is really for intuition only. These are not really probabilities of keeping and discarding because we never actually keep or discard. Instead, what do we actually do is take a mixture of the two components. For instance, twenty five percent of component one and seventy five percent of component two. But we don't actually keep or discard. In actuality, the word gate is very helpful. Imagine two openings side by side. Now, imagine a gate which is the same size as each opening, but can only slide between the two openings. Thus it can only fully cover one of the openings at once, or it can simply cover a part of each. But notice that in total, it always covers an area equal in size to one full opening. In other words, if one opening is twenty five percent clear, the other opening will be seventy five percent clear and they always sum up to one hundred percent. So picture this like an ice cream maker that can give you some mixture of chocolate ice cream and vanilla ice cream. Maybe you like chocolate ice cream more so you choose 90 percent chocolate and 10 percent vanilla sliding the gate to the appropriate point to achieve this. Note that in practice, this is called a convex combination. You can also think of it like a soft mixture, a soft selection. Let's now turn our attention to the other gate vector, the reset gate vector, how does this come into play? Well, first, let's consider how this is calculated. As you can see, it's just another neuron, so that should give you some comfort, there is really nothing new here. As I promised, we're just making use of neurons, which we've already learned about, just neurons connected to more neurons. Now it is called the reset gate vector, which is a good hint about what it's for. Remember that we called the second part of the calculation a simple RNN, but this was not entirely true. This is because this is where the reset gate appears. As you can see, the reset gate is used by doing an element-wise multiplication with h of T minus one. Importantly, remember that the values of r of T are always between zero and one. What happens if we multiply h of T minus one by a value close to zero? Well, it just gets closer to zero. What if we multiply by one? Then it just stays the same as it was before. In other words, before multiplying by the hidden to hidden weight W h h we decide which parts of h of T minus one we want to remember and which parts we want to forget. So we forget them simply by resetting them back to zero, hence the reset gate. Note that this performs a very similar function to the update gate z of T. It's just in a different place. So it's just reinforcing our ability to remember and forget different parts of T minus one. OK, so to summarize what we've learned so far, what is the GRU and why is it useful? The GRU first and foremost has the same API as the simple recurrent unit. The output is still h of T and it still depends on h of T minus one. And accept the difference between this and the simple recurrent unit is it has functionality for remembering and forgetting what was in h of T minus one. This solves a problem we had with simple RNNs where due to the vanishing gradient problem, it would forget things that it saw earlier in a sequence. We accomplish this by adding little binary classifiers in the form of logistic regression neurons that output a prediction on whether to remember or forget.
