In this lecture, we are going to continue our discussion of the LSTM and GRU, previously we discussed the GRU and now we are going to move on to the LSTM. To recap, what did we learn about the GRU? First we learn that the simple RNN unit by itself is problematic because it can't remember long term dependencies. The way we solve this is we make the hidden state the weighted sum of the previous hidden state and the new value for the state, which is essentially the same calculation as the simple RNN unit in this way the GRU always has the opportunity to remember the previous hidden state allowing it to carry that state forward in time, reducing the chance of forgetting it later. Importantly, we recognize that these gates, which decide whether we should remember or forget, are just binary classifiers. There are little logistic regression neurons, something we are very comfortable with. Now we are going to move on to the LSTM, which is a little more complicated, but follows the same idea. Interestingly, when GRUs first came out, the initial research suggested that there was no clear winner between the two. It was reported that the GRU performed comparably with the LSTM. This made the GRU a great choice because it has less parameters and therefore is more performant than the LSTM. These days, the current belief is that this is not true and that the LSTM actually ended up being better. In fact, at the time I am making this course, this latest research only came out about a year ago, which is actually two years after I made my first RNN course. So that just goes to show how fast things move in this field. Experimental results are always changing our thinking about best practices and which techniques to choose over others. This also is a great example of my rule machine learning is experimentation and not philosophy. I know for a lot of beginners, the approach they take is a philosophical approach. They would try to use logical reasoning to deduce which is better. The LSTM or the GRU. The LSTM has these merits, the GRU has these merits and so on. Such things are useless. Please don't waste your time on philosophy instead follow the example that these researchers have set and use experiments to decide which is best. There are two papers I've attached an extra reading that text that you'll want to check out. The first is called on the Practical Computational Power of Finite Precision RNNs for language recognition. And the second is called massive exploration of neural machine translation architectures. They both conclude that the LSTM outperforms GRUs. And so given the choice, I would probably choose the LSTM by default. So how does the LSTM work? Basically, you can think of it as like the GRU but with more state vectors and more gates, again, it's my preference to understand the LSTM through the equations. But if you find these visualizations helpful, then you can feel free to look at that as well. The first difference with the GRU and the LSTM is that the LSTM has two states in addition to h of T, which we call the hidden state. We also have c of T, the cell state. Sometimes the cell state is considered an additional head and state. So you actually might pass both of these on to the next layer. For us, we will usually ignore the cell state so you can think of it more like an intermediate value that you calculate, just like the gate vectors. So you calculate it, but you don't actually use it to pass on to the next layer. So even though the LSTM has an extra step, you can still think of it as having almost the same API as a simple RNN and GRU. It still outputs the final hidden state h of Big T. It's just that for the inputs, in addition to x of one all the way up to x of Big T and the initial hidden state h of zero. We also have the initial cell state c of zero for the outputs. It is a little strange due to how PyTorch works, basically will get H of big T and C of Big T, but the details might be surprising, but we'll discuss that more later in this lecture. OK, so let us get to the LSTM calculations. I want to remind you that while this might seem complicated, it's not don't be scared by the sight of equations, but instead try to see the forest for the trees. Each of these is just a neuron. Once you start to realize that each thing here is a binary classifier or logistic regression, it becomes a lot simpler to interpret. So what do we see? First, we see that there are more of these gates. Specifically, we have f of T the forget gate vector. Next we have i of T, the input gate vector, also known as the update gate vector, analogously to the GRU. And next we have o of T the output gate vector. So hopefully this is the easy to remember because the word forget starts with f the word input starts with I and the word output starts with, oh, next we have the cell state c of T. You might notice that this actually takes on the role of h of T from the GRU. Specifically, we have the weighted sum of two terms. The first term is just the previous cell state c of T minus one. How much of this we end up keeping is controlled by the forget gate f of T. So control is how much of C of T minus one we want to forget. The second term is the simple RNN. How much of this we end up keeping is controlled by the input gate. I have t and notice that this has exactly the same equation as the simple RNN. Unlike the GRU. Now note that for the simple RNN. We have the activation function F of c this can be anything but usually by default is the tanh. Finally we have the hidden state h of T, which is just a simple transformation on the cell state c of T in particular, we apply another activation function F of H, which also can be anything but by default, it is also usually a tanh. We then multiply this by the output gate o of T. So the output gate controls which values of the cell state we actually pass through to the hidden state h of T. Note that in PyTorch, it is not possible to choose F of c and F of h individually and in fact, you can't even change them from the default, as mentioned before, because RNNs are so complicated, they're usually programmed all in one module for the sake of efficiency, and they're not really composable like the other modules we've learned about. Of course, if you were writing your own LSTM, you could customize this any way you wanted, but its performance would most likely be suboptimal. So you can see that by building up our knowledge first through simple RNNs, then GRUs, then LSTMs, we can make something complex like the LSTM seem very simple. It's nothing but three logistic regressions or neurons to give us the forget gate, the input gate and the output gate. Then the cell state is the weighted sum of the previous cell state and the simple RNN weighted by the forget gate and the input gate. And remember, we want to offer the cell state the possibility to remember its old state so that we can learn long term dependencies. Finally, the hidden state h of T is just a squashed version of the cell state with the output gate controlling which values are allowed to pass through. By the way, I say squashed because we use the tanh activation by default and it's not possible to change. So this is really not a hyperparameter you have to play around with. In terms of code, how do the GRU and LSTM work as promised? These have the same or similar API as the simple RNN. So if all you wanted to do is plug in a GRU or LSTM in place of a simple RNN, it can be almost as simple as changing the name. Let's start with how to instantiate a GRU and LSTM here. As you can see, it is almost exactly the same as a simple RNN. We pass on a number of input features d the number of hidden features M and the number of RNN layers to stack L. I also pass in batch first equal to true so that all my data is always N by something instead of having the N dimension somewhere else. The crucial difference is that in a GRU and LSTM, there is no nonlinearity argument because it's not possible to change. Let us now talk about how the GRU and LSTM will be used in the forward function. First, let us discuss the initial hidden state and what to pass into the RNN. Conveniently, the GRU has the exact same interface as the simple RNN as the input we pass in the data into the first argument and the initial state h naught into the second argument. As before, the initial state h naught is of shape L by N by M number of layers, by number of samples, by a number of features for the LSTM, we also require an initial cell state, luckily because the cell state has the same dimensionality as the hidden state. We will also initialize this to L by N by M.. Now, let's talk about how to interpret the outputs from the GRU and LSTM, as you recall, RNNs in PyTorch return two things, not just one with the Elman unit we get one h, which is of shape N by T by M, which tells us the hidden state at the final RNN layer for each sample, each time step, each feature. The second h is of shape l by n by m which tells us the hidden state at the final time step for each sample, each RNN layer, each feature. In the GRU it works exactly the same. In the LSTM, we have something similar, but not the same. The first thing that has returned is the same as what we get with the Elman unit, the hidden value at each sample, each time step each feature. The second thing is different. We get the hidden state h and the cell state c, but only at the final time step. So this second h will be of shape L by N by M, which tells us the hidden state at each sample, each layer, each feature, we also get the cell state of the same shape, which means it is the cell state at each sample, each layer and each feature. Unfortunately, I'm unaware of how you would get the cell states at different time steps.

In this lecture I want to discuss some other ways you might generate multi-step forecasts. You may have noticed that the two forecasting methods we used in this section demonstrated some pretty extreme results. On one hand we saw that one step forecasts can seem artificially good especially when all they do is just predict the last value or close to it. On the other hand doing a multi-step forecast iteratively using the models own predictions can lead to poor results even on simple problems like the sine wave. Even a nearly perfect sine wave model eventually breaks down due to the build up of numerical precision errors at this point. One issue we have to think about is practicality. In fact it's not necessarily wrong to predict only one step ahead. It's certainly wrong when you want to make a conclusion such as Wow look how good my model is at predicting future values. Of course that doesn't make any sense because you used future values to predict the future values. In some cases it may make sense to only want a prediction for one time step ahead. In other cases it may not make sense. For example if you want to forecast weekly or monthly sales for the next year it doesn't make sense to only do a one step forecast. On the other hand maybe you just want to predict the load on your website for tomorrow. So you know how many Amazon machine instances to spin up. Either way the method you use is highly dependent on context and the real world constraints of your problem. It's also important to benchmark your predictions against a baseline model. The reason you want to do this is well what if your complicated model performs worse than your baseline model. If that happens then you should just use your baseline model as you'll see. Sometimes you can even prove mathematically that your baseline model is better than your complex model. One way to establish a baseline is to use what is called a naive forecast a naive forecast does the dumbest thing possible. You guessed it it just predicts the last value of the time series. It's a model with zero parameters. One interesting fact you will learn about if you ever study finance is that stock prices very closely follow A Random Walk Model in a random walk model. A naive forecast is in fact the best forecasts you can make. So by definition if your time series follows a random walk it doesn't matter how complex your model is. You cannot beat a naive forecast in time series literature classic statistical models such as ARIMA use algorithms that predicts only one step ahead and then use the iterative method we discussed previously in order to do multi-step forecasts into the future. One interesting question to ask is Are there any models that naturally predict multiple steps into the future. The answer is yes and we can do so quite trivially. As you know it's very easy to specify the number of outputs in your neural network model. You're just passing a number into the dense layer for the number of outputs you want. So what if you want a model that predicts 12 time steps ahead simultaneously. In fact that's entirely possible. Just make a neural network with twelve outputs. Then as the target you will use the true values for the next twelve time steps. So whereas in this course the target just had one value for a multi head model. You'll have a target with 12 values. If you're interested in this kind of thing you might want to give this a try as an exercise to summarize this lecture what we wanted to do was clarify the difference between the different kinds of forecasts. The big mistake a lot of people make is they pretend they are predicting the future when in actuality they are only predicting one step ahead. It's not wrong to predict only one step ahead but you must be clear about the results you are presenting. If you really want to forecast multiple steps into the future then you are not allowed to use data from the future. Of course there are some cases where you actually want to make one step forecasts only. This is dependent on the specifics of your company and your data only you know that and you must design your model accordingly. We also discussed the importance of establishing a baseline which in time series analysis is often the naive forecast where all we do is predict the previous value of the series I mentioned the random walk model which often very closely models stock prices a naive forecast is in the best forecast. In addition we saw that aside from building a one step model and then iteratively applying it to predict multiple steps into the future there is an easy modification we can simply use a neural network with multiple output nodes representing the multiple steps in the future that we want to predict.

In this section of the course we are going to discuss how to deal with text data in natural language processing. This directly ties into the previous section which was on using RNNs for modeling sequence data. Of course text is also sequence data but there is a major difference between text sequences and the continuous valued sequences we were dealing with in the previous section. That differences. Text is made of words and words are categorical objects. In other words they are not continuous suppose we're given a sequence of words. The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog so x1 equals the X two equals quick and so on. But here's the problem we know that in order to calculate the output of an RNN unit we have to multiply each x by the input to hidden weight W x h. You can see that if X is a category this is not possible you might think Aha I've seen this before when I have categories all I need to do is one hot encode them. So for example what you would do is create an array which has length equal to the size of our vocabulary. In other words the number of words in the English language. Typically we denote that with a capital letter V. So here is how we are going to one hot encode a word. First we're going to create a vector of size Big V containing all zeros. Then we're going to create a mapping where we have for each word a corresponding integer starting from 1. So for example the word a we'll get the index 1 The word A will get the index two the word activation might get the index 100. And we do this for all other words. So we get all the way up to Zu which maybe has the index 1 million finally. Once we have a map for each word to an integer we simply set that corresponding index to 1. So as you can see all of these vectors are a bunch of zeros with only a single one at a unique position so thus our final one hot encoded word vector becomes a vector of mostly all zeros except with one one. So what happens after we do this. Well now we can go back to our usual scenario if we have a sequence of T words and each of them becomes a vector of size V then we have a t by V matrix which represents our sequence. This is the same shape as our generic t by D sequence. We can then pass this into our recurrent neural network as normal. So let's do a very simple example. Suppose we had the sentence I like cats. This is a sequence of length 3 because the sentence has three words. This might turn into the sequence of vectors 0 0 0 1 0 1 0 0 1 0 0 0. For this simple example we assume that our vocabulary only contains four words which of course is much smaller than a real English language dataset but there are some problems with this approach. Some English language data sets have about 1 million possible tokens or words that would lead to an extremely large one hot encoded feature vector which means that your weight matrix would also be very large. So in other words you have a t by V matrix but V is a very big number. In actuality the English dictionary contains only about two hundred thousand words so it really depends on how you split up your words and where you obtain your vocabulary from. But this is still a significantly large number. Here's another problem with this approach. Remember that we would like our input features to have some structure. If you recall one of the earliest rules we encountered was machine learning is nothing but a geometry problem. This rule relies on the fact that there's geometrical structure in our data. Data vectors from the same class are probably close to each other but what do one hot encoded feature vectors look like. Well if we take any to one hot encoded feature vectors and we calculate the Euclidean distance we will always get the square root of 1 squared plus 1 squared which is just the square root of 2. It doesn't matter which two words we select because they are all one hot encoded. For example the distance between Cat and feline would be square root of 2. But the distance between Cat and airplane would also be square root of 2. In other words this data has no useful geometrical structure. So what can we do instead. Well it would be nice if for each word we could map them to a D dimensional vector. Luckily we have just the tool for this. It's called an embedding layer. Now you might be wondering how can we actually make these vectors have a useful structure. We'll get back to that later. So stay tuned. But before we discuss that I want to show you a little coding trick so consider what happens if we multiply a 1 Hot encoded vector with a weight matrix. Let's suppose the vector is just three dimensional 1 0 0 and the weight matrix just contains the numbers 1 up to 9. You can verify for yourself that when we multiply this vector by this matrix we get the vector 1 2 3 now consider the one hot encoded vector 0 1 0. What happens when you multiply this vector by the same weight matrix. We get the vector four 5 Six now consider the 1 Hot encoded vector 0 0 1. What happens when we multiply this vector by the same weight matrix we get the vector 7 8 Nine. So what is the pattern we see if the index in the one hot encoded vector which was set to 1 was 1. Then we get the first row of the weight matrix. If the index was set to 2 then we get the second row of the weight matrix. If the index was set to 3 then we get the third row of the weight matrix. In other words if we one hot encode the integer k and multiply it by the weight matrix. All that is really doing is selecting the k th row of the weight matrix. So here's a shortcut. The old way of doing this took two steps. First we had to create a one hot encoded vector and set the k th entry to 1. Second we had to multiply this one hot encoded vector by the weight matrix the shortcut way of doing this takes only one step. We simply index the weight matrix at row k. This is obviously much more efficient than creating a one hot vector and then doing matrix multiplication. Think of it this way indexing an array is O of one that is constant time. But how long does it take to create a one hot vector and then do matrix multiplication. If your vector is of size V and the weight matrix is a size v times D then this is o of V times D. So this is exactly what the embedding layer in PyTorch does. Instead of doing all the work yourself to create one hot encoded vectors the only step you need to do is map your data set with sequences of words into a data set with sequences of word indices. Now that you have only integers you can use an embedding layer to map each word's integer to a corresponding word vector. From there on out your sequence becomes a T by D matrix at which point you can use an RNN as you normally would Conceptually you can think of the process like this. First we have some sentence a sequence of words let's say for simplicity's sake it's I like cats. Then this sequence of words becomes a sequence of integers. Obviously it doesn't matter which integer we assign to each word as long as they are unique. This is just like when we are doing classification. It doesn't matter if we set dog to 1 and cat to 0 or vice versa. They are just arbitrary assignments. Finally we can use these integers to index an embedding matrix which will convert each integer into a word vector. So in the end what we have done is two steps. First we converted words to integers. Second we map those integers to vectors one question you might have at this point is we know intuitively that similar words should be closer together than dissimilar words. In other words these feature vectors should exist somewhere meaningful relative to each other. For example King should be close to Queen and car should be close to automobile but Queen should not be close to car and King should not be close to automobile so how can we make sure that that's the case. Luckily this is the same story as with convolutional filters because they are just weights in a neural network. They all get trained automatically. There is nothing fancy you need to do. Now there's one caveat to that which is that what people often do is use pre trained word vectors. How this works is when they create an embedding layer. They set the weights to a set of pre trained vectors that were obtained through some other method then they freeze this layer so that those weights are never changed. Typically these word vectors are found through algorithms such as word2vec and GloVe. Now that is a deep topic in itself. So in this course we are going to avoid discussing that. Instead we will train embeddings like any other layer by letting gradient descent do its magic if you want. You're encouraged to read the word2vec and GloVe papers since they are generally pretty accessible. To summarize this lecture here's what we discussed. First we recognize that it is not possible to multiply a word by a weight matrix. There is no concept of multiplying words. Therefore we needed to somehow convert words into a numerical representation we first thought about one hot encoding each word. But we soon realized why that would not be a good idea. First of all it would take up way too much space. There were around 1 million possible tokens in the English language so each word would take up 1 million numbers to represent which is quite silly. Also these one hot encoded vectors are actually meaningless in terms of being feature vectors. This is because each word vector if it's just a one hot encoded vector would be equal distances apart so cat is the same distance to feline as it is to airplane. So that's not very useful. It doesn't allow us to really make use of the rule. Machine learning is nothing but a geometry problem. And thus we need a better way to convert words into vectors. This method is to take each word turn it into an integer and then use that integer to index an embedding matrix. This is much faster than one hot encoding and then doing matrix multiplication in this way. An input sentence consists of words then becomes a T by D matrix of numbers which you know an RNN can readily accept. We saw that this layers parameters are trained just like any other layer. So nothing other than gradient descent needs to be done. Alternatively if you were interested you're welcome to read up on word2vec and GloVe which provide different ways of initializing word embeddings so that you don't need to train them along with the rest of the neural network.

We haven't discussed how to create such sequences of integers yet but I assume you have some idea in your mind what is cause how exactly that will work in a later lecture. But for now we'll just focus on the model itself. So let's start with the constructor as you might expect. It's pretty similar to a regular RNN but just with one additional embedding layer because we have this additional embedding layer we'll also need additional hyperparameters specifically the size of the embedding dimension which we will denote as D as a hyperparameter. Do we want the word vectors to be of length 20 or length 50 or maybe length 300. This is a hyperparameter choice to be made by you. We'll also need to know the size of the vocabulary which will denote as V. So why do we need to know V and D well this specifies the size of the embedding matrix which will be of shape V by D. It has V rows and D columns. Why is that is because each row gives us back a D size vector corresponding to a word. This is what we discussed in the previous lecture. So in total we have five different numbers that we pass into the constructor V which is the vocabulary size D which is the embedding dimension M which is the number of hidden units L which is the number of hidden layers and K which is the number of outputs. Then we instantiate three modules the embedding module the LSTM module and the final linear module. We already know how the LSTM and linear layer work. So I assume this requires no further elaboration. Next we have the forward function in the forward function that we take in some kind of x and then we pass it through each of our layers that we defined earlier since our model includes an LSTM. We know that we need to instantiate an initial hidden state h naught and an initial cell state c naught as usual. The important thing to pay attention to is shapes. First what is the shape of X that we expect as input since each sentence is a sequence of word indexes which are integers. We expect X to be an array of shape N by T containing integers. Each row is a sequence of length T and each of the T columns contains a word index after passing this through an embedding layer. It is going to map each word index to a D sized vector. Therefore we get back an N by T by D tensor. We should recognize this as the usual shape that we pass through an RNN therefore after this. Nothing else really changes when we pass in an N by T by D through an LSTM we get back an array of size N by T by M if we do a global max pool or we simply take the final hidden state we get back a 2D array of size N by M. Finally after passing this through the final dense layer we get back an array of size N by K.

In this lecture, we are going to discuss how we can use convolutional neural networks for sequences, specifically text, although the type of CNN we are about to discuss will work just as well for generic sequences to. You might be wondering, how can this be if CNNs are for images? How is it possible for CNN to also work with sequences? First, let's recall the basics of convolution. The idea is this you have an image, which is the big square. You have a filter, which is the small square, and you're going to slide the filter along each possible position in the big square. And at each point, you're going to multiply all the overlapping values and add them together just like a DOT product. Now, I know this is obvious, but it's worth taking note of an image has two dimensions, height and width. There is also the feature dimension. But that's not an actual dimension which has correlation. And recall what I mean by correlation. If you have a picture of a red car and you find a pixel in the image which is red, probably the neighboring pixels are also red. In other words, pixels beside each other likely have similar values. Now, think of a sequence, unlike an image, a sequence has just one dimension that is not a feature time. So it's time instead of space. But notice one important detail. We have the same type of correlation and sequences, data which are nearby. Other data in time are also close in value. That's why this appears like a smooth curve rather than just noise jumping around with random, uncorrelated values. This suggests that convolution might be useful here as well. Luckily, convolution in one dimension is actually much simpler than a convolution in two dimensions instead of a big square. We just have a big line and the filter is a smaller line. Then we slide the small line across every position in the big line. Multiply all the overlapping values and add them together. Let's do a simple example for the sequence data we have. One, two, three, two, one. And for the filter, we have simply plus one, minus one as an exercise. You might want to try to figure out the answer first before we move on to the solution. OK, so here's what we get at the first position we have. One times one plus two times minus one, which is minus one. At the second position, we get two times one plus three times minus one, which is minus one. At the third position, we get three times one plus two times minus one, which is one. And at the fourth and final position, we get two times one plus one times minus one, which is one. So essentially exactly what we would expect. As with images, it's possible to express this operation as an equation. And remember that in deep learning, while we call this convolution, pure mathematicians and statisticians would call this cross correlation. So just keep in mind the sign is reversed as an exercise. You might want to try and confirm to yourself that this equation does, in fact, implement the operation we just performed in the previous example. And remember that another thing we can do is add on features. So imagine X as a T by D array where T is the number of times, steps and D the number of input features. Then imagine the output as another two dimensional array of size T by M, where T is the number of times steps and M is the number of output features. Then W must be a three dimensional array T by D by M. And then we would have the equation that we see here. This is just like convolution with images for a two dimensional convolution. We have two spatial dimensions, plus one dimension for the input features plus one dimension for the output features. So that's four dimensions in total for a one dimensional convolution. We have one time dimension plus one dimension for the input features plus one dimension for the output features. So that's three dimensions in total. As usual, while convolution might seem like an abstract concept. Remember that there are multiple convenient perspectives on it that make it seem like things we are already familiar with. So one perspective is that it's just matrix multiplication. Just like a regular feedforward neural network. Except that we have shared weights in order to take advantage of the special structure and correlation and the data. Another intuitive perspective is that it's just a sliding dot product and the dot product is just a correlation finder. Correlation is just another name for a pattern matching or similarity. So really what we are doing is asking, is this part of the sequence similar to my filter? And thus the filter becomes a pattern matcher or a pattern finder. All these concepts that you learn about convolution before still apply here. All right, so now that you know how Convolution works with sequences, how do we apply these the text? Well, luckily when we use embeddings, that already gives us exactly what we need for a one dimensional convolution. We need an input, which is a T by D sequence, where T is the number of timesteps, and D is the number of features. And of course, this is exactly what we get after we pass our sentence through and embedding layer. We go from a length T sequence of words to a length t sequence of integers to a length T sequence of D length vectors. Since we have T vectors each of length D this makes up a T by D matrix. When you stack them all together and thus we have exactly what we need to build a CNN for text. So here's how it all looks in code. First, we have our input. That's a length T sequence of word indices. Then we have an embedding layer. The output of that is a T by D sequence of word vectors. Then we have a one de convolution. This is just the Conv1d class. Then we follow the same typical CNN architecture where we have convolution followed by pooling and so forth. So the same pattern applies here that we had for images. Generally speaking, the data shrinks in the time dimension, but grows in the feature dimension. So that's why you see the number of feature maps getting larger and larger. Once we've done that, then we can do a flatten or we can do a global max pooling, which will give us a single vector of size M3. Finally, we pass this through one or more dense layers to get a single scalar, assuming we are doing binary classification. As you can see, this is no different from a CNN meant for images, except that all the convolutions and pooling are one dimensional instead of two dimensional. There is one small caveat to what we just discussed. But it's not obvious until we tried to implement the forward function inside the constructor. There's no real problem because all we're doing is instantiating some objects. But remember that in PyTorch, the general convention is that for convolution features come first. We saw this earlier in the context of two dimensional convolution on images. PyTorch Convolution works on images of size and by C, by H, by W, which means that color comes before the spatial dimensions. In other words, a feature comes first. However, in TensorFlow, OpenCV and other libraries will use the convention. And by H. By W, by C. Which means that the feature dimension comes last. torchvision in some sense accepts that this is the convention and makes its interface such that you can work with N by H, by W, by C all throughout your code and never have to worry about the fact that in PyTorch things are backwards. This is because you don't ever interact with the data explicitly torchvision does all that work for you. But now we have this mixture of conventions. The output of an embedding is N by T. By D. Where T is the sequence length and D the feature dimension. So the feature comes last. When it's the output of an embedding. But the Conv1d function, just like the Conv2d function, expects the features to be first. In other words, it expects the features to come before the time dimension. So it wants to see N by D, by T and not N by T, by D. What we end up having to do is permuting the data right after the embedding and before the first convolution. So after the embedding its features last, but before the first convolution, we reshape it to features first. Then after all of our convolutions and poolings have been done, we permute the data back from features first. It features last. At that point, we can pass the data through the usual dense layers that make up the rest of the CNN. So here it is in action, since there are many layers in a CNN. I've split this up to make it more readable. Here we take in the input and pass it through and embedding layer. Then we do a series of convolutions and poolings. I'm not going to show all the convolutions and poolings since we just repeat the same pattern over and over. But we can reason about the shapes. So first, the input X is an N by T array of integers. After the embedding it becomes N by T by D word vectors. Next we permute the dimensions. So it becomes N by D. By T. After the first convolution, we change the number of features. So it becomes N by M by T the ReLU which comes next, doesn't change the shape of the data. After pooling, which changes the length of a sequence we get N by M by T2. You can think of T2 as T divided by two or T divided by three depending on the pooling parameters. Next we go through the second convolution and so on and so forth. So let's pretend that we had a three convolutions. So after the final convolution, our data has the shape N by M3 by T3 at this point, we need the features to be last again. So we call permute again and we get N by T3 by M3 after doing a global max pool along the time dimension we get N by M3, note that because we can specify the axis to perform the global max pool on, we didn't necessarily have to permute the data after the final convolution. You could just choose a different axis. Although I think this makes it more clear what's going on. Lastly, we passed the data through a final dense layer and as usual, we get back an array of size N by K!

In this section of the course we are going to cover one very important topic in a modern deep learning which is called transfer learning. This lecture will introduce you to both the intuition and implementation of transfer learning. So by the end of this you'll be able to understand that the subsequent code. The nice thing about transfer learning is it allows you to obtain very good off often the state of the art results with less effort and less resources spent the intuition behind transfer learning is this. Let's start with the basic observation that in a CNN the features that are learned at each layer are hierarchical. In the beginning layers the CNN only learned some basic lines and strokes in the later layers. The features get progressively more complex from lines and strokes to parts of faces eventually to full faces. This is of course if you train your CNN on images of faces. You can also train your CNN on other types of images as well. Of course but here's another basic observation. We recognize that the initial layers learn to recognize just simple lines and strokes is a plausible that other task that don't involve looking at images of faces would still find a line and stroke features useful. The answer is yes because probably all pictures will have lines and strokes. The difference between a car and a face being that the way that you put together those lines and strokes will be different in this way. We can imagine that the first few layers of a CNN might be useful for a wide variety of tasks from facial recognition to vehicle classification to recognizing anomalies in medical images. This is the basic idea behind transfer learning. It's the idea that the features that I found for one task could be useful for some other task transfer learning really took off in the field of computer vision so that's what we were going to focus on in this course. Probably the most widely known large scale image dataset is called ImageNet. This is a dataset that contains millions of images and 1000 categories meaning it can recognize 1000 different objects. Every year there is a contest to see who can build the best image classifier on this dataset. The nice thing about the ImageNet dataset is because it's such a large dataset containing so many different kinds of images we can transfer the features learned from this dataset to a wide variety of tasks suppose we wanted to build a dog versus cat classifier. That's easy because ImageNet already knows how to classify dogs and cats. Suppose we wanted to build a car versus truck classifier. That's also easy because ImageNet already knows how to classify cars and trucks is even possible for us to use the same features for things ImageNet has not seen before like say images from a microscope all right. So that's just the high level intuition. Let's go deeper and discuss how this will actually work conceptually. First we recognize that it's not feasible for us to train a CNN on ImageNet ourselves although it's a lot less expensive and time consuming these days compared to the earlier days of deep learning in the old days it was common for CNN training to take on the order of days weeks or even months. Nowadays we have distributed training multi GPU clusters and so forth but at the same time it's still not really something you want to do on your own. Luckily many of the major CNN architectures that have won the ImageNet contest in the past have released their pre trained CNNs to the public so there's no need for you to do any hyperparameter tuning. Try out different learning rates and so forth. All that has been done for you and the results are open source doubly awesome is that these pre train networks are already included in PyTorch. We'll discuss what they are and how to get them later let's say you found a super powerful state of the art CNN trained on the ImageNet data set and now you want to use it to do transfer learning for your specific task. How can you do that. Well let's start with the picture. This is a picture of a typical CNN. It's a series of convolutions and poolings followed by a series of dense layers. One perspective on the CNN is that it's made up of two parts part one which involves convolutions and pooling makeup a feature extractor or a feature Transformer. It takes your raw image and converts it into a feature vector which is a useful representation for ANNs and other machine learning models. Part 2 is just a feedforward neural network or ANN which we learned about earlier in this course. We can think of Part 1 as the body and part 2 as the head. So here's how transfer learning works. What we do is we chop off the head keep the body which is a useful feature transformer and then attach our own head. This head can be used for whatever task we want to perform for example identifying cars and trucks. In that case we might use a logistic regression with a sigmoid output since as you recall the sigmoid activation is the appropriate activation function for binary classification optionally you could add more layers to make it a feedforward ANN then here's another important detail about transfer learning. There are a few approaches to this and I'm going to teach you about the most important and the most basic version. The idea is we're going to freeze the weights of the body and only train the head. In other words only train the logistic regression layer. You can imagine that if we use that gigantic pre trained CNN with 100 layers it would train very slowly because we would have to update all the weights of a 100 layers CNN. But by freezing the body we can simply ignore those weights and only train the weights of our own linear model. The important point is we don't need to train the convolution layers because they have already been trained on a data set much larger than anything we could have gathered ourselves. The weights we already have for those convolutions are very good. There is no need to try to make them better. Instead we can assume that they give us good features and worry about training the top one major advantage of using transfer learning is that you don't need a lot of data to build a good model. You might recognize this graph which basically says that the more data you have the better your deep learning model is. This is opposed to classic machine learning methods which tend to plateau after a certain point. So you might think in order to build a good a deep learning model you must have a lot of data which will in turn make your neural network take a long time to train but with transfer learning. This work has been done for us. We don't need a lot of data because the earlier features we're already trained on a lot of data more data than we could have practically handled ourselves and so transfer learning allows us to get the benefits of deep learning without needing to have a ton of data ourselves. And on top of that it means we can train our model a lot faster. Not only are we just training a logistic regression but we have a smaller dataset compared to what we would need if we trained our model from scratch.

Let's briefly discuss a few of the popular architectures that I use for transfer learning. The first and most popular is probably VGG which stands for Visual Geometry Group. This is just the name of the research team that created it. When you look at the architecture for VGG. Although it got state of the art results at the time it's not that different from what we already know. It's just the usual CNN with an unusually large number of layers. At least it was a large number of layers compared to other neural networks. At the time it was created. So here's how it looks. First we have two convolutions followed by pooling. We repeat that once then we have three convolutions followed by pooling and we repeat that block three times. Finally we have three fully connected or dense layers. As you can see it's pretty much the same thing as LeNet just bigger. We have a series of convolutions and pooling followed by a few dense layers. Note that there are a few variations of the VGG network such as VGG16 and VGG19 which have 16 layers and 19 layers respectively. Another common choice is ResNet ResNet is an even larger network than VGG. We won't go into too much detail in this course since our objective is not to understand ResNet but just to know what our options are. The idea behind ResNet is that it's a neural network with branches each branch is responsible for learning something different. It turns out that one of the branches is just the identity function. So the other branch is responsible for learning the residual hence the name residual network like VGG ResNet also has different variations with different numbers of layers. There's ResNet 50 with 50 layers ResNet 101 with 101 layers and ResNet 152 which has 152 layers. There are also some ResNets with different architectures such as ResNet V2 and ResNeXt yet another common choice is inception. The layout of Inception is similar to ResNet in that you have multiple parallel branches but with Inception The concept is a little different with Inception instead of just a single convolution going into another convolution you'll do multiple convolutions in parallel. You recall that one of the hyperparameters we have to choose is the filter size. Well inception says why not simply try them all and concatenate the result. So for example you'll have a one by one filter a three by three filter and a five by five filter and convolve the same input image by all these filters. Once you've done that you'll take the resulting images and stack them all together. The idea behind the inception network is that you'll have multiple layers of Inception blocks just like how the ResNet has multiple layers of residual learning blocks. Now I know a lot of people are going to ask Well which one should I choose VGG ResNet or Inception. And the answer is as always you have to try it on your specific dataset with your specific task. There is no way to predict which one will work better for each use case another popular pre trained model used for transfer learning is called MobileNet which specializes in being lightweight. So this one actually does have a specific purpose because it's lightweight. There's a tradeoff made between a speed and accuracy. Generally speaking the ideal use case for MobileNet is if you want to use convolutional neural networks on less powerful machines such as mobile devices and embedded devices.

In this lecture I want to discuss two different approaches to transfer learning both of which we will cover in the subsequent coding lectures. The main issue I want to cover is this Imagine that the body of our neural network is very large. Let's say hundreds of layers the head as discussed previously can just be a single logistic regression dense layer. The issue is even though we are not training any of the weights in the body it still takes time to compute an output prediction. Just imagine a really big long nested function at each of these layers. We have to do a convolution which is faster than matrix multiplication but still can take a non-trivial amount of time. Imagine this computation in two parts in order to calculate the output prediction. We first calculate a feature vector z using the body of the neural network. Then in order to calculate the output we take Z and pass it through a logistic regression. My issue is the first part of calculating Z is what takes a long time. Now consider that our gradient descent loop works as follows. We loop through each batch of data for each batch. We calculate the output prediction y. Then we calculate the gradient of the error with respect to the logistic regression parameters W and B then we update a W and B using those gradients. The thing we want to think about is this Does the calculation of Z ever actually change since Z is the output of the VGG network. After passing in our input data it doesn't make sense to put this inside our loop because it's going to be the same every time. Remember the VGG weights are not going to be trained. So here's what I propose. Remember my rule all data is the same. The idea is before we even begin training let's convert our image data into a tabular matrix of feature vectors z then all we need to do is run logistic regression on Z without ever looking at the VGG network again. By doing this we can avoid having to pass our data through any pre trained network which can take a lot of time if it has a lot of parameters. All right so there is a problem with what I just proposed. What is it. Well remember that when we create our image data generator it gives us the option to do data augmentation with data augmentation. Every time we loop over the data set the generator modifies the original images just a little bit to help our neural network generalize better. Of course if X is different on every iteration of the loop then Z will also be different on every iteration of the loop. In this case we cannot pre compute Z before the training loop begins. The only time it makes sense to do that is if we don't care about doing data augmentation so these are the two approaches approach number one will be to use the image data generator with data augmentation. This means we have to put the entire CNN computation inside the training loop approach. Number two will be to pre compute the feature vector z on the original data X without data augmentation. This means that after transforming the data all we need to do is train a logistic regression model. There are pros and cons to each approach. Let's list them out as discussed earlier. When we do use data augmentation that means we have to recompute the features for every batch we see. This is slow especially if you have a large network. Yes it's faster than training the entire network but still slower than only training a logistic regression on the other hand. Data augmentation may help your model generalize better without data augmentation. It's basically the opposite situation. You can pre compute the features before training which will save you a lot of time training logistic regression is extremely fast yet. This also means that you cannot use data augmentation which may cause your model to perform sub optimally. However it's always worth trying both to see which method gives you the best results for your specific dataset.

In this lecture we are going to discuss a very popular topic in modern deep learning. GANs GANs stands for generative adversarial network. Yann LeCun who is one of the forefathers of Deep Learning described GANs as the most interesting idea in machine learning in the past 10 years. By the way this is also who the famous LeNet architecture of convolutional neural networks was named after the CNN from which all other CNN's are based. Ian Goodfellow the inventor of GANs is now himself a prominent deep learning researcher. My goal in this lecture is to introduce you to the fundamental theory behind GANs as you'll see that although they sound complicated they are nothing but a new and interesting way of combining things we already know how to build. This is a common pattern in deep learning neural networks themselves are nothing but a bunch of logistic regressions chain together. CNNs and RNNs are nothing but neural networks with shared weights. I like this approach because deep learning allows us to build tons of cool things with only a few simple tools and some creativity. First let's discuss what GANs are even used for in the first place. Since this may not be immediately obvious the main use case for GANs is to generate data. Ninety nine percent of the time. This means generating images. The reason GANs have become so popular is because unlike the models that came before it GANs are exceptionally good at this. Here is some example images produced by state of the art GANs. Believe it or not these are not real people but rather images generated by a computer one thing you can do if you want to see a few more examples and observe for yourself the power of GANs is to check out a few Web sites that display such examples. One Web is. This person does not exist. Dot com. This one is simple. You go to the page and it shows you a randomly generated face. You can refresh the page to see more faces. Another one which I really like is which faces real dot com. This one is more like a game. So you're shown two images and one is real. One is fake and you have to pick the right one. So check these out for yourself. If you want to see more examples of how good GANs are at generating realistic images OK. So what's the main idea behind GANs GANs are a system of two neural networks each of which has their own objective the objective of the first neural network is to generate images. The objective of the second neural network is to discriminate between real and fake images. This is all you need to understand how GANs get their name. They are generative because you are generating images. They are adversarial because you have two neural networks which oppose each other in an adversarial manner. They have opposite goals. The goal of the first neural network is to generate images that look real and the goal of the second neural network is to detect real and fake images intuitively. You can think of GANs like a counterfeiter and a shop owner. The counterfeiter goes to the shop and tries to use fake cash to buy an item. The shop owner has to detect whether the cash being given by customers is real or fake. Perhaps at the beginning both the counterfeiter and the shop owner are not experts at what they do. The counterfeiter is not that good at making fake bills but the shop owner is also not that good at detecting fake bills. However once the shop owner learns to detect the fakes the counterfeiter may then improve on his counterfeit design and trick the shop owner once more. After a while the shop owner may again realize he is being duped and learn to inspect the bills more carefully to detect these improved fake bills. The cycle continues as the counterfeiter gets better at tricking the shop owner and the shop owner gets better at avoiding being tricked. Of course these analogies only take us so far. How do we actually build a GAN. Let's recall all the ingredients we need for a basic neural network that we want to train first. We need a neural network that much is obvious. Well in our case we actually have two neural networks in order to train the neural network. We need an objective or a loss function. This is the big question with GANs. What is the loss function. But once we have these two things everything else is nearly trivial. We call model dot fit which does gradient descent and that's that OK. So let's dig a little deeper on what the loss function is. And in fact for a GAN we're going to have two loss functions one for the generator and one for the discriminator. Let's first look at the discriminator since that's more in line with what we are used to already. Since the discriminator must be able to tell the difference between real and fake images. This is a binary classification problem for every input the discriminator can only predict one of two categories real or fake. As you know for binary classification the correct loss function is the binary cross entropy. What about for the generator. What is the loss function. This is what I call applying creativity to the basic tools that we already know about intuitively. The basic idea is this we have our generator network in our generator network feeds into our discriminator network. From this perspective this is just one gigantic neural network. What we can do is just like with transfer learning we can freeze the layers in the discriminator so that when we run gradient descent only the generator network gets trained next. And here is the ingenious part. We want the generator to get better at producing real looking images. And so our loss function will remain the binary cross entropy except that we are going to switch the labels. In other words let's say for the discriminator real is one and a fake a zero. We're going to pass in fake images but make the target one such that we're encouraging the discriminator to identify these fake images as real but the discriminator weights are frozen so they won't change when we do this only the generator weights are trained here's what the loss would look like mathematically. If you're interested here all the y hats are predictions on fake images. Since the generator is now the input into the discriminator because we always want the target to be one we only care about the first half of the binary cross entropy. So essentially it's just the sum over the log of all the y hats. Or as stated another way the negative log likelihood of the y hats now that you understand the basics of how GANs work. Let's look at some details that will help us in our implementation. We know that neural networks must have both inputs and outputs for the discriminator. This is easy to input as an image and the output is a prediction about whether the input image is real or fake for the generator. This will be a little strange. We know that the output should be an image because its job is to generate images but what is its input. In fact the input to the generator is nothing but noise. What we are going to do is generate noise from a multivariate standard normal and the generator will learn to map this noise to an image. Mathematically what we are doing is saying we have some random vector z which comes from a standard normal. Let's say it has size D equals 100 although this is a hyperparameter so you can choose what you like. We call this one hundred dimensional space. The latent space in essence you can think of it as an imaginary space where the generator believes all the images of digits live. So maybe the ones are over here. All the sevens are right beside it because seven's kind of look like ones near the Sevens or the nines because nines look like sevens if you draw the loop very small so you can see how these images kind of morph into one another when they are drawn in different ways. So this latent space maps all the different kinds of images that you can have and of course this is a source of confusion for both computers and humans. When an image is right on the boundary between say 7 or 1 it's difficult for us to tell what digit it should be. Should it be a 7. Or should it be a one. In any case what the generator is doing is it's learning to associate each part of the latent space with different images in a continuous manner. Then later when we generate images we're just picking a random part of the space and generating an image from whatever that part of the space represents. You can think of the generator as kind of the reverse of a feature transformer or an embedding with a feature transformer or an embedding or taking an input image or an input text or some other kind of input and we're mapping it to a vector. But for a generator in a GAN we're doing the opposite. We start with a vector and then we map that to an image as always it's going to be helpful to look at some pseudocode before we move on to the actual implementation. So here's how it's going to look. So the first step is the load in our data set. We're going to use MNIST for this example in a future courses. You'll learn about more advanced types of GANs which will work on more complex types of data. Next we're going to create our discriminator and generator networks. These are just standard neural networks some dense layers some ReLUs and so forth. The trick is we're going to have two optimizers one that optimizes the parameters of the discriminator and one that optimizes the parameters of the generator. Conceptually you can imagine that the loss function is always applied to the output of the discriminator only in either case we will use the binary cross entropy but with flipped labels when we train the discriminator half of the data will be real images from the dataset and half of the images will be generated from the generator. These will use the true labels when we train the generator we will generate random noise pass that through the generator then pass that through the discriminator and use a flipped label meaning that we say it's a one even though it's really a zero we can conceptualize this chain of generator and discriminator as a kind of combined model where only the generator weights our parameters although that's not exactly how we'll look at code. It's a good conceptual tool. Once we've built our two networks we're going to run a gradient descent loop as usual inside the loop. We're going to train the discriminator and generator in alternating order in order to train the discriminator we'll grab a random sample of images from my dataset and a random sample of images from our generator. Then we'll do one iteration of gradient descent by calling discriminator dot train on batch. We do this for both the real and fake images then for generator training we'll do the following. First of all generate a batch of noise samples then we'll call combined model dot train on batch passing in the noise and ones for the target to do one iteration of gradient descent on the generator. After several thousand iterations our generator should be good enough to produce images that look like the MNIST data set. As a final note for this lecture I want to mention that in terms of model evaluation we're going to take a bit of a departure from what we normally do. You recall that for most models what we're looking for after training is that the loss goes down and the accuracy goes up. This makes sense if you are doing classification or regression but now we are no longer doing classification or regression. Remember that in our case the generator and discriminator are constantly trying to one up each other. And so what is interesting is that the loss functions for both the generator and discriminator should look just like noise. It should appear that if you only look at the loss per iteration that nothing is happening at all. But in fact something profound is happening both the generator and discriminator are improving. You don't see this in the loss per iteration because ideally both the generator and discriminator are improving at the same rate. Let's now summarize everything you learned in this lecture. First you learn that GANs are not just a single neural network but a system of two neural networks a generator and a discriminator. The discriminator is responsible for telling the difference between a real and fake images. The generator is responsible for creating realistic looking images both the generator and discriminator learned in tandem. The loss function for the discriminator is just the binary cross entropy because there are two classes real and fake the loss function for the generator is not directly applied to the generator but rather a combined model where the generator feeds into the discriminator. This allows us to again use the binary cross entropy. But there are two important details first we freeze the weights of the discriminator so that only the generator is trained. Second we flip the labels so that image is generated by the generator are labeled as real. Next we learn that the input to the generator is nothing but noise sampled from the latent space the latent space is where the encodings for each digit live. You can think of this as the opposite of a feature transformation or an embedding and embedding or feature transformation is like a mapping from an input image or an input word or any other kind of input into a single vector. The generator does the opposite. It takes a vector which lives in the latent space or the embedding space and produces an image. Lastly we learn that when training GANs the loss per iteration should not be informative in the sense that it should not decrease over time as it does when we are training other models. This is because both the discriminator and the generator should be learning at the same rate continually helping each other improve.

This is the centrepiece of this section because unlike all the previous examples you saw in this course this training loop will be very different from what you saw before you may have assumed that because the generator is a kind of a. Discriminator that they would have opposite architectures. What I mean by that is if the generator had hidden sizes of one hundred three hundred and seventy four that the discriminator would have hidden sizes of seventy four three hundred and one hundred. In fact this need not be the case in our example we'll make the generator a more powerful model than the discriminator. The intuition is binary classification is an easy task whereas generating images is a hard task for the discriminator. All you have to do is map the input to 0 or 1. There aren't that many degrees of freedom for the generator. You have to generate seven hundred eighty four different pixel values and they all have to be coherent. So there are many degrees of freedom. So that's the idea generating is hard but discriminating is easy. So here's what we'll be using for the discriminator although you should feel free to play around and design your own. It's just a series of linear layers followed by leaky ReLUs. Recall that a leaky ReLU is just like a normal ReLU except it has a small positive slope for values less than zero. This is an attempt to avoid the problem of dead neurons where the slope becomes zero and therefore the gradient becomes zero and therefore no error can back propagate here's what the generator looks like. Again feel free to play around. So in addition to leaky ReLU using linear layers we'll also add batch norm to the mix. We've also added a tanh activation at the end which implies that we'll be working with images in the range minus one plus one rather than zero to one experimentally. Researchers have found that these changes tend to yield better results. OK so here's the real meat of this code. After we define the discriminator D and the generator G we're going to define the loss and optimizer the loss is just the usual binary cross entropy. But we're going to have two separate optimizers one for each network. You'll notice that when we instantiate the optimizers we only pass in the parameters that we want the optimizer to update. So when we call D optimizer dot step it's only going to update the parameters of the discriminator when we call G optimizer dot step. It's only going to update the parameters in the generator inside the training block. We're going to start by instantiating constant arrays to store zeros and ones. These will act as our targets. So we don't have to keep creating new arrays on each iteration of the training loop inside the training loop. We're going to loop over the data loader. Remember that we don't need the image labels so we can use an underscore to ignore them what we're going to do now is two training blocks one for the discriminator and one for the generator. This slide will focus on the discriminator. Now one question you probably have is does it matter which order you train them in the discriminator first or the generator first. I would recommend you try it out as an experiment so how do we train the discriminator. First we start by passing real images into the discriminator. That's just the outputs from the data loader. From this we can calculate the loss using the ones target for the fake images. We start by generating a batch of random noise and then passing that through the generator. From that we get fake images which we then pass through the discriminator. And from that we get fake outputs. We pass the fake outputs through the loss function using the zeros target next. We take the average of the two losses to get a single value. We can optimize. After this we would like to call d loss dot backward and d optimizer dot step. But before that we have to remember to zero the gradients next. Let's look at the generator training block. One interesting technique discovered by researchers was that doing multiple steps of training for the generator for each single step of the discriminator seemed to work well. This goes along with a theme that the generator is harder to optimize than the discriminator. Therefore it requires more training so to accomplish that we can just do a loop inside the loop. We generate some fake images once again using a batch of latent noise and passing this through the generator. Since this is for training the generator there is no need to use any real images. We just passed the fake images through the discriminator and then passed that output through the loss. Importantly this time we use the ones target to tell the loss function that we want the weights to go towards these images being classified as real. Next we zero the gradients and do a gradient descent step as usual.

In this lecture we are going to look at how to implement a GAN in code. This lecture is gonna walk you through a prepared Colab notebook. So if we take one subtract a mean of zero point five and divide by a standard deviation of zero point five we get zero point five divided by zero point five which is one if we take zero subtract the mean of zero point five and divide by a standard deviation of zero point five we'll get minus zero point five divided by zero point five which is minus one. Therefore we map 1 to 1 and 0 to minus 1. So this works. Next we load in the MNIST train dataset from torchvision. You've seen this before. Next we set the device to be the GPU and we move both the discriminator and generator to the GPU. Next we create a loss and optimizers for the loss we can use the binary cross entropy for both cases. The only thing that changes is the label for the optimizer as we make sure to pass in only the parameters for that specific network. So the D optimizer only optimizes the parameters in the D model and the G optimizer only optimizes the parameters in the G model. Next we have a convenience function for scaling images back from minus one plus one to zero one. This is useful for plotting and saving and so forth. Next we create a directory to store the images generated during training is called GAN images. Next we have the training area. So this will be slightly more complex than the code preparation section. Sort of start we're going to create one dimensional arrays just containing ones and zeros. These will be used as targets during training. The targets are constant values so instantiating these inside the loop would be wasteful. Next we create two lists to store the losses for the generator and discriminator. Next we enter a loop that will go for two hundred epochs and inside that loop we have another loop to go over the data loader notice we ignore the targets by using an underscore since they are not used inside the loop. The first thing we do is get in the batch size. Next we create our fake images by passing this noise through the generator. Next we pass the fake images into the discriminator and we get the fake outputs. We pass the fake outputs into our criterion with zeros as the target. We'll call this loss D loss fake. Next we combine the losses by taking the average then we zero the gradients in both optimizers. Then we call the loss dot backward and then D optimizer dot step to do one step of gradient descent on the discriminator. Next we have the train generator block. As mentioned it's been found that training the generator more than once for each iteration is useful. So we do a for loop that goes twice inside the loop. We generate some random noise of size N by one hundred and move that to the GPU. Next we pass this to the G model to get a set of fake images. Next we pass the fake images through the D model to get a set of fake outputs. Next we pass the outputs through the criterion this time using ones as the targets. This is because we would like the discriminator to think these are real. Next we do a gradient descent step. First we zero the gradients. Then we call G loss dot backward and then we call G optimizer dot step and remember that even though the outputs that go into the loss function are outputs from the discriminator we are running G optimizer which only knows about the G models parameters so only the G models parameters are updated. Finally we save the losses to our list of losses. I want to begin by thinking about supervised learning when we think about say an image classifier. You can think of it as a static function. I pass on an image and I get a prediction. It tells me what kind of object is in the image. For example there is no notion of time I pass in another image. I get another prediction. The image classifier is just a function I given an input and it produces an output so what do I mean by static. And what do I mean by time. You might immediately think of recurrent neural networks which are neural networks that can handle sequences inputs that vary with time. However this is not the kind of time I am thinking about if I pass in some stock prices for a given time period and my model predicts whether the stock will go up or down tomorrow. That's still a static function. Here's what I mean by time. Imagine you are building a self-driving car simulation at each moment in time your neural network can take a snapshot of the screen and decide what to do next. Should I steer left. Should I steer right accelerate or brake. So this is the difference between a supervised and reinforcement learning supervised learning is just a function you can call this function repeatedly but it's still just a function you pass in an image and it produces an output reinforcement learning is more like a loop. It exists to achieve some goal. For example driving you to your desired destination inside the loop yes it still takes in an image and produces an output that specifies how to control the car but importantly this reinforcement learning program has the concept of time. It doesn't think about just what is this image. How do I translate this image into an output prediction. Instead it has the capacity to plan for the future even though at this moment the car may only see where it is on the road right now. It knows that there is some sequence of actions it must take in the future that will lead it towards its goal. All right so that's the major difference between a supervised learning and reinforcement learning with supervised learning. We have no concept of a goal or the future or planning. We just take an input and produce an output. It's a static function. With reinforcement learning we have a plan and that plan can be carried out in the future to reach some predefined goal here's another way to think about reinforcement learning. Think about the data with supervised learning. Again let's use image classification as our example. We must have a label for every input in our training set. So if we have an image of a dog we must have another item specifying the class dog. If we have an image of a cat we must have another item specifying the class cat. In other words for every x we must have a Y it's important to remember that label data sets must be made by humans. Why is this important. Well think about our self-driving car again. Take this image of the road. If we were to use supervised learning for this data point we would need to give it a target. But what's the target. Should I steer left. Should I steer right. Should I accelerate. Should I brake. In fact you probably cannot give this image a target and even if you could how could you possibly label every single frame that the car will encounter along its journey. Imagine if you have a standard camera that captures images at 30 frames per second and you have a one hour drive as your data set. One hour is thirty six hundred seconds which means you would have to label one hundred eight thousand images from just one trip instead. Reinforcement learning learns using goals rather than targets. For example suppose you wanted to teach a reinforcement learning algorithm to solve a maze. In this scenario the goal would be finding the maze exit. You do not need to tell the algorithm what the correct thing to do is for each position on the Maze. Since that would be supervised learning instead the only thing the reinforcement learning algorithm needs to know is what is the goal from there.
