In this lecture we are going to define a one more term which deserves its own lecture so far. I told you that the goal of the agent is to maximize the reward it gets. But as you recall the reward may be structured differently in different games. For example in tic tac toe you may receive a plus one for winning or a minus one for losing on the other hand. If you're solving a maze you might get a minus one at every step. So what does it mean to maximize the reward. Does it mean to maximize the reward at the next step. Or does it mean to maximize the total reward over an entire episode. Here's the answer to stated more accurately the goal of the agent is to maximize the sum of future rewards. Why is that. Well it can't maximize the rewards it got already. Those are in the past. They cannot be changed. Furthermore we don't want to only maximize the reward on the next step. What if we are solving a maze and we get a minus one for any step we take. In that case the agent isn't incentivized to do anything useful because no matter what it does the immediate reward is still minus one. Thus the agents true goal is to maximize the sum of future rewards until the episode is over. In this way the agent is planning its future steps as well. It must have some concept of where it will end up because that's the only way it will know how to maximize rewards in the future to take a real world example. Consider again the idea of preparing for a math exam for a math exam. You don't receive any reward until you've completed the exam. The reward signal is your grade on the exam. But imagine all the actions it will take to actually maximize that reward. You'll have to study you'll have to do homework. You have to forgo socializing with your friends. In fact all of those actions do not sound very rewarding at all and thus if your only incentive is immediate gratification. In other words the rewards you receive immediately. Then you will not do well on your math exam. Instead you must make use of long term planning. Sure I may not want to study today. It may be very annoying and I will miss my favorite TV show. But because you are planning long term you're not thinking only about today. You're thinking about the results of your math exam. The desire to maximize the total future reward is necessary for long term planning we call the sum of future rewards the return we describe the return mathematically. Using the symbol G because it depends on future rewards only it is time dependent. So we index it with a T. We can say the return at time t is the sum of rewards at time T plus one up to the terminal state at time big T now you might be wondering what happens if we have an infinite horizon MDP a game that never ends. We introduce a discount factor called gamma. Each future reward is weighted by gamma to some power gamma is usually a number close to one like zero point nine zero point nine nine or zero point nine nine nine. It's a hyperparameter so you'll have to choose its value based on the performance of your agent. The idea is the further you go into the future the harder it is to predict. Therefore we care a little more about getting rewards now than we do later. Intuitively this works just like money. I would rather receive one hundred dollars today than receive one hundred dollars ten years from now. In ten years 100 dollars will be worth much less than it is today due to interest one important feature of the return which we will make use of throughout the rest of the section is that it can be defined recursively. In other words in terms of itself specifically the return at time t is equal to the reward at time T plus 1 plus gamma times the return at time T plus 1. To end and summarize this section I want to discuss at a high level what it takes to learn it reinforcement learning for real. Personally I think it would be quite difficult to grasp reinforcement learning and understand it on an abstract level from just a single section of a single course let's start by recognizing that reinforcement learning is very different from supervised and unsupervised learning. Nowadays when you're studying supervised and unsupervised learning many beginner courses take the approach of avoiding how to implement the models. This is not a good approach because it doesn't prepare you for understanding real machine learning. Let's suppose the structure of the courses like this First you discuss the intuition behind how the model works. Just some pictures and some descriptive ideas. Then you learn how to use that model in scikit-learn not including loading in the data or looking at the results. So what is the problem with this approach. Well it allows you to not only make many mistakes and have serious misunderstandings about the content but perhaps the biggest problem with this approach is that you will never know what those misunderstandings are. In other words you are in a place where you don't know what you don't know. You don't know your mistakes and hence you can't fix them. You're confident that you've learned something but this is nothing but blissful ignorance and again these are just my observations of other students. So don't take it as a personal judgement of you. This is not so much a problem. If that's how far you want to go if you only ever plan on using APIs and you'll never want to become an actual professional that's totally fine and nobody is judging you but it becomes a problem when it's time to stop using APIs. This turning point appears when you want to learn how to do reinforcement learning. There is no API for reinforcement learning at least not yet. So what is one to do. Well you have to implement those algorithms yourself. The problem is if you have no experience implementing machine learning algorithms reinforcement learning is not a good place to start. I want to also comment about the many blogs tutorials and so forth that exist out there attempting to teach you about reinforcement learning. Consider how long it took us in this section to go from nothing to deep Q learning at a pace that I would consider as fast as possible. Compare that to the length of a typical blog tutorial. It should be clear that it would be impossible for a short blog post to include enough detail to get you to the point where you can actually implement reinforcement learning yourself. The best advice I can give you if you want to learn reinforcement learning for real is this. I would recommend taking a full course or multiple courses about reinforcement learning. Learn about basic tabular reinforcement learning before you move on to approximation methods that will make understanding the concepts much easier in this section we spent most of our time discussing the concepts under the assumption that we were using a Q table and not a neural network. You want to learn about the basic approaches to reinforcement learning which can be categorized into number one dynamic programming methods. Number two Monte Carlo methods. And number three. Temporal Difference methods. And make sure to spend some time on implementation after that. Move on to approximation methods with linear models. Once you've done that and you've implemented it reinforcement learning algorithms with linear models move on to using deep learning for function approximation at this point you should be very comfortable with the concepts but implementation is still another matter entirely. Unlike supervised and unsupervised learning reinforcement learning is very hard to get right even if you are an expert programmer. It is very easy to introduce subtle bugs that are difficult or nearly impossible to track down and of course you don't have to take my word for it. Here is a post by Andrej Karpathy probably one of the most famous reinforcement learning researchers talking about just how difficult it can be and this come in another user talks about how they spent an entire year trying to get Q learning to work with neural networks for a particular game. Many students who take my courses get frustrated when an exercise takes more than a few minutes. Now imagine working on something for one year Andrej responds to this comment and says it took me six weeks to get policy gradients working and keep in mind he's one of the world's leading researchers in reinforcement learning. He has all the state of the art technology he needs on demand and he's surrounded by other researchers who are just as smart as he is so he can ask them for advice or to check his code at any time. So the key idea I want you to keep in mind is that as you learn reinforcement learning realize that implementation is very non-trivial even for experts. You should expect to spend a lot of time and effort trying to get things right.

In this lecture I'm going to introduce you to the next project of this course. Creating a reinforcement learning trading bot. Usually when people think about applying machine learning to the stock market they usually think about it in terms of predicting the value of a stock which includes even just the direction like whether it will go up tomorrow or down tomorrow. Of course that information by itself doesn't do anything physically. You still need to sit down at your computer and make a trade. If we're talking about automated high frequency trading then that's a different story. Even so let's say your model predicts that the stocks you are looking at will go up tomorrow. Does that mean you'll make a trade. Maybe. But what if you're busy and you forget. Or what if you believe it's going to go up only slightly and then decrease rapidly then probably you don't want to buy that stock. This is the key difference between a traditional supervised and unsupervised learning versus reinforcement learning supervised learning only makes a prediction. It doesn't actually take any action based on that prediction. I can predict tomorrow's stock price but I still have to choose whether I will act on that information or not. Reinforcement learning on the other hand not only makes predictions but also takes actions in the environment that you provide. So in this section of the course we are going to study how a reinforcement learning algorithm might take such actions in a stock trading environment let's just go over a rough outline of how this is going to work. Currently you probably just think of stock prices as a simple time series data set at this time it has this value at the next time it has this other value and so on. That sounds more appropriate for a recurrent neural network rather than reinforcement learning. So what makes this a reinforcement learning problem. Well it's a matter of perspective. Imagine let's say you're hooked up to a stock trading API using this API you can call functions which do real world financial transactions. So if I call the buy function passing in the argument GOOG and 10 that means I'm going to buy 10 shares of Google stock. If each share is worth fifty dollars that means five hundred dollars is going to be deducted from my bank account and instead I will now own it 10 shares of Google let's say I call the sell function and I pass in the argument AAPL with the number five. That means I just sold five shares of Apple stock. If one share of Apple is worth thirty dollars then I will now receive one hundred fifty dollars in my bank account and I will own five less shares of Apple stock than I did before. Importantly you can see that the act of calling these functions is an action you might think of your state as information such as recent stock prices. How much cash you have to buy my stocks. How many shares of each stock you own the values of those stocks and so on. The environment is the actual stock market. It's inherently random because you can't really predict what's going to happen to tomorrow's stock price but your actions affect the environment. In other words these are all the ingredients we need to specify our problem as a reinforcement learning problem. We can perform actions such as buy and sell in the environment and our state is made up of information about various stocks in our own portfolio and the environment is the stock market itself. The reward is some function of the money we made or lost something useful to try. Which is probably something many of you have done already is to think about how you yourself are a reinforcement learning agent. When you are looking at a stock and trying to decide whether or not to purchase some shares you generally want to follow the rule buy low sell high. So for example here we can see a dip in value. This would be a really good time to buy. And here we see a peak. This would be a really good time to sell well. Only if you need the money. Hopefully you are investing in something where the general trend is always going up. So if you don't need the money then the best thing to do is just let it sit and continue to increase in value. Of course the problem is that in the real world you are trying to make these decisions without knowledge of the future. How do you know if the most recent price is a dip or a peak. In fact we do not. And so perhaps this is a job best left for the machines.

Now it's We're thinking about how well we calculate the value of our portfolio as an example suppose we own 10 shares of Apple 5 shares a Motorola and 3 Shares of Starbucks. The corresponding share prices are 50 dollars for Apple twenty dollars for Motorola and thirty dollars for Starbucks. Let's also suppose we have one hundred dollars in cash not invested in any stock. Then the total value of our portfolio will be ten times 50 plus five times 20 plus three times 30 plus 100. That's equal to seven hundred ninety dollars in general. If we store the shares we own in a vector called S and we store the corresponding share prices in an array called P and we store the amount of cash we have in a variable called C then the total value of our portfolio can be calculated as follows. It is equal to the dot product of S and P plus C the reward then we'll just be the difference between these two. Comparing the most recent timestamp and the previous timestamp to summarize this lecture let's recap the important points about the environment and its implementation. First our environment will be an object that mimics the OpenAI Gym API so it will have functions like reset and step which returns all the information we need to implement our reinforcement learning program. Next for our environment we'll be considering three stocks Apple Motorola and Starbucks next. Our state is a vector with three pieces of information. First it includes the number of shares of each stock that we want to consider. Second it includes the share price for each of those stocks. Third it includes the amount of cash we have that's not invested in any stock. Next our actions are a simplified subset of the large number of actions we can perform in the real world. We also assume there are no transaction costs. Simply put we have three options for each stock buy sell or hold. We'll take an all or nothing approach where if we buy we're going to buy as many shares as possible and if we sell we're going to sell all of the shares we own. And these actions can be applied in any combination for each stock we own. So if we're considering three stocks then we'll have three to the power three possible actions you'll notice that even with just three stocks and a much simplified action space we still have quite a large number of actions so if we have N stocks we would have three to the power N possible actions. It grows exponentially with the number of stocks we own. So encoding the actions in this way will not scale. If we have many stocks to consider finally the reward is just the change in value of our portfolio from the previous steps to the current step. The value of our portfolio is just the price of each stock we own. Times the number of shares we own plus any uninvested cash we have.

In this lecture we are going to discuss how to implement a replay memory or replay buffer efficiently to understand why we would want to do this. Let's first consider how we might implement a replay buffer using a naive programming approach. Once we've done that we'll discuss why it's not ideal and then move on to a better version. In essence a replay buffer is simply a python list. Inside this list we are going to store tuples with five elements each s a r s prime and the done flag. So as our agent takes a step and encounters a new tuple it will just store this tuple in our list. The buffer of course has a maximum size. So once we've hit the size limit we're going to throw out the oldest value. How do we do that. Well we can use the python function pop and passing the argument 0. This means remove the element at index 0 next. Let's consider how we will use the buffer during training. What we would like to do is grab a batch of random samples from our buffer. From this we can calculate input target pairs and then do one step of gradient descent. Remember that the target will be calculated as our plus gamma times the max over a prime of Q of s prime a prime and this only applies if as prime is not a terminal state. Otherwise the target is just the reward by itself. In other words we're going to do some kind of calculation over the batch of data we just sampled. Here's how you might do this. Start with an empty array of targets. Then loop through each of the tuples you sampled for each iteration check whether the done flag is true or not. If it's true then the target is just R. Otherwise it's just the formula we saw previously. Of course as you may know we don't like doing for loops in Python. If we can avoid for loops we'll be slower than doing batch operations in NumPy. It's true that you could gather the batches together and cast them into a NumPy array but that means you still had to store a bunch of lists not ideal here's another problem with continually appending a new tuples and popping old ones. It may seem like this will take up only a constant amount of memory since the memory storing the old removed values should be freed by the garbage collector. Unfortunately python will not do this and you will end up with a memory leak and a very slow computer. This probably won't be an issue with a modestly sized dataset like the one we have but it's good to be aware of the kinds of problems that may arise when you want to graduate to more advanced applications. So what's the solution the solution is to implement your own replay buffer. Here's a high level view of how it'll work. First we're going to pre allocate the arrays we will use to store the states actions rewards and so on. So this will really take up a constant amount of RAM. We will never allocate new arrays nor try to remove any arrays. All we will do is populate our pre allocated arrays. Second we'll use a pointer which will tell us the current insertion location of our transition tuples. So every time we encounter a new tuple we'll store it in the next available location in the array. Now what happens when the array is full. Well the oldest value is at the beginning. So that means we can simply overwrite it in this way our buffer is circular. When we get to the end we just go back to the beginning. In this example you see here we can see that the pointer shows us the value at the current time t. But before that we have the value at the previous time. T minus 1. This goes back to T minus 2 T minus 3. But whereas T minus 4. In fact it's at the end of the array because when we store the value for T minus 4 we were at the end. So the next value T minus 3 would have been stored at the beginning since we had to circle back to replace the oldest value on the next step. We would replace the current oldest value which is at T minus nine one small detail. We have to think about is what happens when the array is not yet full. In this case we will still need to keep track of the current size of our buffer. For example the pre allocated array may be of size 10 but we will only have store 5 values than the effective size of the buffer will be 5. When we sample a batch from this buffer we can only sample values from zero up to 5 so that's it for this lecture instead of using the naive approach of storing our transitions in a list then sampling from the list to get yet another list. We will instead use a fixed size array and store transitions in this fixed size array in a circular fashion.

Next, we create an argument parser object, so that we can run the script with command line arguments. We'll have one argument, the mode where we can pass in a train or test. Next, we create the model directory and rewards directory in the case where they do not yet exist. Next, we call the getData function to get our Time series. We call the shape attribute to get the number of time steps and the number of stocks. Next, we split the data into train and test, the first half is train and the second half is test. Next, we create an instance of our environment objects with the training data. After that, we get the dimensionality of the state and the dimensionality of the action space. We pass these into the agent constructor to get the agent. We also called get Scaler to get the scalar objects. Next, we initialize an empty list, which will store the portfolio values for each episode we play. Next, we have an important if statement, this is going to overwrite some of the things we just created in the case where we are in test mode. So if we're in test mode, we want to use the scalar that we had during training so that the neural network corresponds with the same scalar and we don't accidentally use a different scalar. Next, we recreate the environment with the test data rather than the training data. Also, we have to make sure to set Epsilon to a small value. Otherwise its default value is one which is just pure exploration. Note that if you set it to zero, there is no point in running multiple episodes because both the data and our agent will be deterministic. So you'll get the same result each time. Finally, we have to make sure we load up the weights that we saved during trainings, we call agent load and pass in those weights. Next, we enter a loop to play our episodes, num episodes times. Inside the loop. We grab the current time since we would like to know the duration of each loop iteration. Next, we play one episode and receive the portfolio value at the end of the episode. Then we get the current time and subtract the start time to get the duration of the episode. Next, we print out all this information, the episode number, the portfolio value and the episode duration. Next, we append to the portfolio value to our list of portfolio values. Next, we check if the mode is train, at this point, we are finished playing all of our episodes, so if the mode is train, then we'll save our neural network to a file called dqn.h5 will also save a scalar to scaler.pkl. Lastly, for both train and test will save the rewards we got so the train data will be saved in train.npy and the test data will be saved in test.npy. In this lecture we are going to look at a slightly more advanced topic in PyTorch which is creating custom loss functions. In addition we're going to apply this new knowledge to build a new kind of neural network one that not only estimates a function but also estimates the uncertainty in the function prediction previously. We spent the entire course only looking at neural networks that act as function approximators for each input. We get some output prediction but you may have noticed something curious. There is in fact a discrepancy between a regression and classification with regression. We only get one answer. The model's output is our best guess for the target given that input. But with classification we get a probability distribution. This probability distribution gives us some sense of the confidence in that prediction. For example if we're doing binary classification and the output is zero point nine nine then we might conclude that our model is very confident in that prediction. If the model outputs zero point five five then it would still make the same prediction. But intuitively we know that we are less confident in that prediction. You can apply the same reasoning to softmax outputs. So given this knowledge you might wonder why don't we output probability distributions when we're doing a regression so if you've studied regression and the mean squared error more in-depth then you know that doing regression with the squared error is nothing more than maximum likelihood estimation with maximum likelihood estimation. We start with the likelihood. Take the log of the likelihood and then negate the likelihood to make it a loss to minimize rather than a utility to maximize in this form. We say that T which is the target is the random variable which we assume comes from a Gaussian distribution. Y is the model prediction which is the mean of the distribution and X is the input to the model we call theta. The collection of model parameters. So this can represent a neural network linear regression or any other regression model. Doesn't matter as you've seen the usual first step is to take the log of this function at this point your gut instinct should be this. We know that we want to end up with the T minus Y squared term and all the other terms should drop off. That's what gives us the sum of squared error or the mean square error and we know that we can do this because the log of 2 pi sigma squared is constant constants don't affect the gradient of the loss. So whatever model parameters maximize this log likelihood would also maximize the log likelihood minus or plus any constants but here's the major difference in this lecture in this lecture. We are not going to make Sigma a constant. Instead we can ask what if sigma is also a function of x. So now this term can't be dropped from the objective function because it is not constant. What this means is that in this scenario this whole thing will be our loss function instead of just the squared error. And as usual we can take the mean instead of the sum which is equivalent to having a Monte Carlo estimate of the expected value. The next question you should have is OK now we're trying to predict two things the target and its corresponding variance. How can we do something like that. Well why not just have a neural network with two output nodes. Let's remember that it doesn't matter what the meaning of these two output nodes is. We've seen that a neural network can end with a linear layer with any number of output nodes. That's the case whether we're doing regression binary classification or multi class classification. So then what's the difference between these three cases. The difference is that the meaning is assigned by us the designer of the program and we assign that meaning through the loss function. In other words it's up to us to come up with the appropriate loss function such that the meaning of these two outputs is the Gaussian mean and variance but you should be suspicious at this point. A neural network layer can output any value but don't we have a constraint on the value of a variance. In fact we require that a variance is positive in order to enforce the variance to be positive. We can make the assumption that the neural network doesn't output the variance directly but rather the log of the variance if you think hard this is just like the classification case. The neural network doesn't output probabilities directly. Instead it outputs logits which are related to log probabilities. In fact that has more constraints because not only do probability distributions have to have positive values they also have to sum to one using this information we can determine what the loss function should look like with respect to the neural network's outputs. First let's assume that instead of having a neural network with two output nodes we simply have two neural networks in our model and then the forward function returns the output from these individual neural networks then the output of our model from the forward function will be a tuple with the first element is the mean predictions and the second element is the log variance predictions. Now we get back to our original question which was how do we create a custom loss function in PyTorch. As always it's easiest to start with what we're familiar with the mean squared error. If we had a regular regression neural network that only outputs the mean prediction then here's how you would do it. The trick is there is no trick. The lost function is merely a regular Python function that takes in any arguments you want. Obviously some of them have to be PyTorch variables for us this means the predictions and the targets then inside this function we find the element wise difference between the predictions and the targets square them and then take the mean. Pretty straightforward so a custom loss function is just a regular function that does mathematical operations using PyTorch. So how do we do this. When it comes to the full negative log likelihood First we still take in the same arguments the predictions and the targets. This time the predictions are tuples so we can split them up. The first element becomes the mean which I'll call mu and the second element becomes the log variance. Since the exp function is the inverse of the log function I can take the exp of the log to get the variance itself which I'll call V then we simply need to plug and chug into our formula for the negative log likelihood. This consists of the coefficient term and the exponent term since we're in log space. We can just add these two together and this gives us the element wise negative log likelihood after which we can take the mean so at this point you may be wondering how is a model like this useful. And naturally you can apply this technique to any problem that contains uncertainty in the target function if we recall the bias variance tradeoff. This is the statement that the error of your model is the bias squared plus the variance plus an irreducible error the irreducible error is called that because it's a characteristic of the data itself and your model can't make a perfect prediction because of it. This arises naturally. For example suppose you're measuring the relationship between how long students study on a test and the grade let's say you have one student who study 10 hours and got a ninety five percent. And you have another student who study 10 hours and got an 85 percent. In this case the input is the same but the target is different. And since your model is only a function of the inputs it can't make a perfect prediction. If there are two different possible target values for that single input as you can imagine this kind of noise can appear everywhere. So instead of ending with a generic statement like my model has a low R squared you can quantify the uncertainty of your model instead when the variability of the target. With respect to the input is not constant. We say that it's heteroskedastic we can think of other situations where heteroskedasticity can arise. One popular application is with stock returns and stock prices. These are well known to be heteroskedastic in finance. We often want to avoid high variance because we think of variance as risk. And so in order to minimize risk we should minimize variance. And in order to minimize variance it would be useful to model not just the prices of the returns but the variance itself.

In this lecture we are going to look at the code to demonstrate uncertainty estimation using PyTorch. This lecture is going to walk you through a prepared Colab notebook. Although a very good exercise which I always recommend is once you know how this is done to try and recreate it yourself with as few references as possible as usual you can look at the title of the notebook to determine what notebook we are currently looking at. So let's begin by writing a function that generates data from a known synthetic distribution. This might seem weird but in fact this is exactly what we do when we run an experiment or do data collection. It's like we have some function called generate batch and that function is a black box which involves whatever data generating process happens to result in the data you're measuring. Of course the difference is that you don't ever know the true distribution of your data nor the underlying data generating process. And that's why we need machine learning. But for this example we do know the true distribution and the data generating process and hopefully that will give you some insight on what machine learning is trying to do. So what does this function look like. First we generate a bunch of random points for the input x from the uniform distribution between minus five and plus five. Next we write an expression for the standard deviation as a function of x. As you can see it's a linear function of x. So when x is small the standard deviation is small and when X is large the standard deviation is large. Next we get the target we assigned the target to be the cosine of X minus some linear function of x plus Gaussian noise center at zero with a standard deviation of SD. Then we return x and y if we plot the data you should be able to recognize each of these elements. First we can see the periodic component due to the cosine. That's why this thing appears like a wave. Second we can see that a trend downward. Thanks to the linear component. Finally we see heteroskedasticity. The noise seems to increase as X increases. In fact we know that the noise standard deviation increases linearly with X. Importantly we can see here that given the same X it's possible to get many different values for the target. Next we create our model. This is a pretty basic custom model which contains two simple ANNs. The first ANN will be used to predict the mean of the output and the second ANN will be used to predict the log variance in the forward function. You can see how this is kind of the opposite of a recommender system. A recommender system takes in two inputs a user and an item and returns one output a predicted rating on the other hand. This takes in one input and produces two outputs. Next we instantiate the model and then we create our custom loss. So in this function we'll stick with the convention of calling the first argument outputs and the second argument targets inside the function. We know that outputs is a tuple with two components. So we take the first component and assign that to a variable called mu. We take the second component exponentiate it and assign that to a variable called V. Next we calculate the coefficient term of the Gaussian distribution. That's the log of the square root of two pi times V. Next we calculate the exponent term of the Gaussian distribution. That's zero point five divided by V times the square difference between the targets and mu. Lastly we add the coefficient term and the exponent term together and take the mean. Next we have our optimizer and our training function. So this is nothing really new. All right. So here's our loss per iteration. There should seem a little strange since what we're used to when we look at a loss per iteration is that the loss usually has a steady decrease downward. This on the other hand seems to be very noisy. So what is the cause of all this noise. Well remember that our data itself has noise and the loss function is the negative log likelihood. Remember that the loss doesn't only contain just the squared error anymore. So we shouldn't expect the loss to go down to zero since that would mean the variance is zero which we know is not true. Next we plot the model predictions in order to do this. We're going to generate a large batch of 1000 twenty four points after doing a scatter plot. We convert these points into torch tensors reshape them and pass them through our model. The model returns two things our y hats and the log variance. Since our model outputs the log of the variance we can exponentiate it to get the variance but that's not actually what we want. If you recall the variance doesn't have the same units as the original random variable so it doesn't make sense to plot them together. Rather we would like to plot the standard deviation which is the square root of the variance equivalently. We can just divide by 2 before taking the exponent since the square root is the same thing as a power of 1/2. Next we plot our prediction along with the corresponding uncertainty on top of our scatter plot of the data in order for a plot to look like it should we have to sort the data points first. This is because matplotlib joins the points you pass in by a line in whatever order you pass them in we can get the sorted index by using the argsort function. Next we plot X versus Y. This should follow the center of the data points for each X. Next we use the fill between function to draw a transparent band with width equal to the standard deviation so that's why we have y hat minus SD and then y hat plus SD. So here's the plot and as you can see the band increases as we go from left to right and our model accurately predicts that the variance should increase as X increases.

In this lecture we are going to discuss the theory behind the facial recognition approach. We are going to take in this section at this point. I hope you have given some thought as to how you might approach facial recognition if you had to create your own implementation. I think this is a worthwhile exercise especially if you've never seen any facial recognition approaches before. This is kind of a one time opportunity because once you do learn about how facial recognition is currently done it will taint your thinking. So take this time to think about how you would approach facial recognition without any external influences OK. So now that you've had the chance to think about how you might approach facial recognition let me describe to you what most might consider a good first crack at this problem. Facial recognition seems like nothing but image classification. Suppose for example our school has 100 students and given an image of a face. Let's suppose we want our neural network to tell us which student that is so we might build a CNN with 101 classes where the extra class would be for images of faces which are not one of the 100 students. Now this is not necessarily a bad approach but there are some issues. For example what if one student leaves the school or another student joins the school. Now we would need to build a new classifier or what if we need our neural network to recognize millions of people having a neural network with millions of output classes is generally not a good idea. In this section we are going to take an approach similar to binary classification. Suppose we have some neural network where we can feed in two images the output of the neural network is just a binary decision. Are these two images of the same person or not. The architecture we will use for this approach is called a Siamese network. This is of course named after the famous Siamese twins. The idea is this we are going to have two CNNs with the exact same shared weights. Hence they are twins. Both of these CNNs are not classifiers so they don't have any classification head and they don't end in a softmax. Instead the final layer is just a linear regression with no activation which just outputs some feature vector here's what we'd like these CNNs to do if we input two images of the same person even if they are different images we should get feature vectors that are very close to one another. So the CNN would have to be trained to ignore things like lighting conditions different angles different face sizes. Maybe one day you are wearing glasses and one day you are not. And so forth. In other words the CNN has to learn the features that are actually distinctive to your face not other differences in images on the other hand if we input two images of different people the feature vectors should be far apart. So even if the two images have the same lighting conditions are at the same angle have the same size and so on the CNN should learn how to distinguish those two faces using the actual features of those faces. You can think of this in terms of word embedding. We know that after training an algorithm like word2vec or GloVe we can map words into a vector space. Similar words appear close to one another. While dissimilar words appear far apart. For example fish should be close to carp and laundry should be close to dryer whereas fish should be far away from laundry in the same way the Siamese network outputs face embeddings. These are simply a mapping from an image of a face to a feature vector at this point. You may be wondering once we've converted both input faces into feature vectors. What do we do with them. I said earlier that we would do something like binary classification. Well in fact there's nothing stopping us from doing exactly binary classification. So let's say we take these two feature vectors and then we calculate the absolute difference between them to give us a new vector. Then we simply pass this new vector z through a logistic regression. In this way we are doing exactly binary classification. Now you might wonder why should we take the absolute difference. Well this is because if we input image one into the first neural network and image 2 into the second neural network it should give us the same feature vector. If we reversed the images so we input image 2 into the first neural network and we input image 1 into the second neural network. The difference between these two images should be the same in both cases and thus the feature vector must be symmetric another option here is to build the feature vector using something called the chi square similarity which uses the formula you see here. Basically it's just a different way to calculate the features you should confirm to yourself that the chi square similarity is also symmetric but for our coding exercises I would actually like to show you a different approach. This uses what is called the contrastive loss and it accomplishes exactly what our intuition wants us to do. Remember the idea is that images of the same person should have feature vectors which are close together whereas images of different people should have features which are far apart. So how can we push the feature vectors closer together or further apart. The answer is the contrastive loss. So how does the contrastive loss work. Well it helps to look at the formula. Basically it looks like what you would get if you combine the squared error with the binary cross entropy which kind of makes sense because this is a binary problem but we are also working with continuous feature vectors. First let's talk about how it works and then we'll talk about why it works. So let's discuss all the variables. What does D that's the Euclidean distance between the two feature vectors or the two embeddings. You can also think of this as the L2 norm of f of x 1 minus f of x 2. Next what is y y is the target it's 1 if x 1 and x 2 are images of the same person and 0 otherwise next what is m m is what we refer to as the margin. This is the key ingredient of this loss. We'll discuss this more when we talk about why this loss works finally. Note that this loss is specified for a single training sample which consists of a pair of images x 1 and x 2. So if we have multiple training samples then we would just take the mean of this okay. So now that you know what each of the variables in the loss means why does it actually work. Let's look at the first term since it's a little simpler. It's y times D squared. Remember that y can only be one or zero it's one when the two images are of the same person. Therefore when both images are of the same person only the first term matters and we want D squared to be small. We want to minimize D squared if both images are of the same person. The other scenario is when we have images of different people when y is 0. Only the second term matters. Notice how we are taking the max of m minus D and 0 basically it say if D is bigger than M then m minus D will be negative. So just take the loss to be zero. Thus it saying if we have two images of different people we want D to be large but as long as it's greater than or equal to M we don't really care how large exactly it is. So we don't want to push D to infinity just bigger than M is good enough. What is the result of this loss. Well hopefully if we draw a histogram of the distances we get when we feed in images of matches and non matches it will look like this. You can see that we get two distributions. The distribution for the matches should hopefully be very close to zero and the distribution for the non matches should hopefully all be equal to or greater than M. The idea is once we can see a plot like this we know how to classify whether or not two images are a match. We can choose a threshold for example with this plot. That might be zero point seven five. Then when we plug in two images into our Siamese network and we get a distance less than zero point seventy five we can predict that they are a match. If it's bigger than zero point seven five we can predict that it's not a match. As a side note you can see that we are going to set m to 1 which seems to work well enough for this problem. You are of course encouraged to try different hyperparameters on your own.

As I mentioned in the introduction to this section the theory behind Siamese networks is not all that difficult. It's more complicated than a CNN you would use for image classification but it still follows the same steps. We have a system of CNNs we set up a loss and then we minimize that loss. Relatively straightforward. The real challenge here is what do we do with the data. Normally when we train a CNN for image classification we have a simple dataset of input target pairs for x. We have a single image and for y we have the class which the image belongs to. But what happens with a Siamese network. We don't have any label for a specific image necessarily or at least not the labels we will use directly here's what will be given. We're still going to get a list of images for each image. We will be told their identity. For example the first image belongs to subject one. The next image belongs to subject 2 and so forth. But these are not the labels that the Siamese network cares about. Remember that what we care about is if two pairs of images are a match or a non match. So how do we do this what we have to make our own dataset to keep things simple let's say we have three subjects and we have two images for each subject. Let's call these images a b c d e and f so A and B belong to subject one C and D belong to subject 2 and E and F belong to subject 3. Now this becomes a counting problem. What are all the possible ways we can combine these images into pairs if you recall when we have N images. We should end up with N choose two pairs. So let's see what we get. We get a AP AC A D E and F then we have b b b b and b f then we have c b c and S.F. Then we have D E and F and then we have just e f. And of course we have the corresponding labels. So a matches with B C matches with D and E matches with f all other samples are non matches. You will notice a problem which is inherent in the way that this data is created. It's that we will always have a much higher number of non matches than matches. In other words we will always have imbalanced classes. So if we tried to train the Siamese network with the usual batch gradient descent we are going to see a lot more of the non match class than of the match class to solve this problem. We are going to do two things first because we always have N choose two combinations of images. There will always be many more training samples than actual images. We don't want to store all those pairs of images in memory because that would be redundant. We would just be storing the same images over and over again. Thus we want to create our own generator and loop over that inside our training function. This will allow us to generate the data on the fly and not have to store it in some gigantic matrix. Second by running our own generator. This offers us some flexibility. What we're going to do is for each batch we'll take say 32 images from the match class and then we will sample 32 images from the non match class. In other words for every epoch we'll be looking at all the matches but only some of the non matches so far a simple example earlier where we had the images A B C D E and F here's what we would do. Only a b c d and e f are matches all the other training examples are non matches. Now let's say we do a gradient descent with a batch size of six then three training examples from the batch would be the matches a b c d and e f the other three training examples would be chosen randomly from the non match class. So let's say we choose AC DC and b f. Of course this means that on each epoch we will always see all of the matches but only some of the non matches in the following lectures we will look at the actual code to see how the process we just discussed is implemented.

In this lecture we are going to summarize everything we learned in this section of the course. This section was all about facial recognition with Siamese networks. One thing you saw in this section was that while the theory was relatively simple the implementation was complex not because of the model itself but because of all the data processing Siamese networks by themselves are quite simple. We passed two images through the same CNN and this gives us a face embedding for both images. Then we would like to know the distance between these two embeddings just like we do with word embeddings that tell us how similar the two faces are if the two faces are so similar that the distance between the embeddings is less than some threshold and we predict that they are the same person. If the faces are from different people the distance between the embeddings should be greater than the threshold so that we can predict that they are different people in reality. Suppose you are running some kind of facial recognition database at your company instead of always passing in two faces at a time something simpler you could do is just store the embeddings themselves in a database. So for all the employees of the company or all of the students in a school don't store their images just store their embeddings then when it's prediction time you only have to calculate the embedding for the incoming image and compare that to all the existing embeddings in your database to determine which person it is. Next we looked at all the data preprocessing steps of which there were many. First we loaded in the data and split the images up into train and test. It was important to realize that the data being fed into the neural network itself not be split up but rather we should split up the images to start with. This is so that none of the images in the train set will appear in the test set and this is because the actual data set we train the neural network on simply consists of the same images being paired up amongst themselves multiple times. We don't start with a lot of images but we end up with a lot of training samples which grow quite dramatically with the number of images we have. Next we looked at how to convert the data into pairs. There are many ways of doing this and sometimes it can be difficult to try and understand what someone else's approach is. So as always the most important thing is to code it up yourself. This always leads to the best understanding next. We wrote some data generator functions so that we could iterate over these in our training loop to generate data on the fly and not have to store them in gigantic Redundant Arrays. Finally we wrote a function to help us evaluate the Siamese networks. In particular it would draw a histogram of the match distances versus the non match distances and prints out the sensitivity and specificity. This is better than accuracy because we have imbalanced classes due to the nature of the data. We will always have more samples from the negative class than the positive class.

In this lecture we are going to discuss the mean squared error in depth the goal of this lecture is to ensure that you understand the mean squared error from a probabilistic perspective. This helps to give some theoretical backing for the mean squared error and it will help prepare us to discuss the cross entropy loss as well as a side note. I just want to remind you that there are multiple names that we use interchangeably. So if you hear error or loss or cost or objective. These are all generally referring to the same thing. So we might say cross entropy error but we also might say cross entropy loss they mean exactly the same thing. First let's just make sure the mean squared error makes sense in the first place. Why is it squared. Well the idea is that we would like the error to always be positive. Imagine this scenario one of your predictions has error plus 2. The other prediction you've made has error minus 2. If you add these two errors together you would get plus two minus two which is yes zero. Of course this is not zero error because both of your predictions are off by 2. They should not cancel each other out. So squaring the error is a nice way to make it positive but this still doesn't really explain why we want the square rather than the absolute value. Why not some other method of making the difference positive. In fact it's perfectly OK to use the mean absolute error. We just don't normally refer to that as linear regression. So when we say linear regression usually we are talking about a linear model using the mean squared error. OK so let's dig a little deeper on why we would want to square the error to understand this discussion. You have to be familiar with maximum likelihood estimation what you would normally learn in an introductory probability course. Let's say for example we would like to measure the heights of all the students in our class and we decide to model this as a Gaussian distribution. As you recall the Gaussian distribution is the typical bell curve. It has the probability density function that you see here which will become important momentarily. We know intuitively that the best way to estimate mu let's call that mu hat is the sample mean of all the heights we have measured. The question is why is this so here's how we solve this problem. There is actually a method to find this mu. This method is called maximum likelihood estimation. As I mentioned earlier. So what are the steps. First we create the likelihood function let's call that L. Unfortunately we use the letter L for a lot of things and deep learning. So please don't confuse this L with anything else we've discussed. In this lecture we are going to discuss the binary cross entropy loss which is the correct loss function to use when we are doing binary classification. Let's recap the actual loss function and then we will use the rest of this lecture to determine how to arrive at this loss function. Since we know that this is going to be based in probability let's think about the associated probability problem. We know that the outcomes the Y's must be binary. That means the targets in a binary classification problem must be 0 or 1 spam or not spam fraud or not fraud etc.. The next question is what distribution is used for binary events. The answer is the Bernoulli distribution probably the most typical example of the Bernoulli distribution is the coin toss. So imagine if you tossed a coin a bunch of times and you want to calculate the probability of heads. Call that mu. Intuitively we know that MU is the number of heads divided by the total number of coin tosses. Again we are going to go through the process of maximum likelihood estimation to see how we can arrive at this answer. All right. So let's say we've tossed our coin a bunch of times. Let's call the results x1 x 2 all the way up to X N. In this case the x i's can only take on 2 values 0 or 1. Let's say 1 means heads and zero means tails in order to calculate the likelihood we need the Bernoulli PMF which is the equation you see here now there's one small difference between this example in the previous example on the squared error. The difference is that for the previous example we were working with heights which are continuous valued. Now we are working with coin tosses which are discrete a coin toss can only give you 0 or 1. It can't give you say zero point five zero point nine. So we know from my study of probability that for continuous distributions we use the probability density function but for discrete distributions we use the probability mass function or PMF. So this is a PMF and it returns a probability rather than a probability density since you already know the steps. Let's get right to it. We create our likelihood function which is the product of the PMFs for each of the x's we've collected. We know that we want to maximize the likelihood but the step we have to do before taking the derivative is that we want to find the log likelihood at this point this equation should already look very familiar. It's in the exact same form as the binary cross entropy except it negated as usual if you were to take the derivative of the log likelihood set it to zero and solve for mu. This is what you would get. Curiously we arrive at the same answer as the Gaussian case the sample mean of x. How can this be. Why isn't it. Number of heads divided by n. In actuality it is. Remember that X can only take on the values 1 and 0. So when x is 0 that's tails. So they don't contribute anything to the sum of X the sum of X then is just the sum of a bunch of ones which is the number of times we flipped heads. So in fact this is exactly the same as number of heads divided by n as before. If we take the negative log likelihood and we put it side by side with the binary cross entropy we can see the similarities. We can conclude that what the binary cross entropy is really saying is that y is the result of a coin toss with a probability of heads for that coin toss is given by y hat i. Analogously x i is the result of a coin toss where mu is the probability of heads for that coin toss as a side note. You want to keep in mind that we also usually divide the sum of the errors by N so that we get the average binary cross entropy per data point. This makes it just like the mean squared error in that the value is invariant to the number of samples we have. You can imagine that if we have lots of samples and we only use the sum the error would be very large only due to the fact that we have a large number of samples in order to make the value of the error more meaningful. We can take the average and that makes our error more interpretable So to conclude what have we done in this lecture. We have shown that just like the mean squared error the binary cross entropy loss function is based in probability. What it says is that for the regression case where we use the mean squared error it arises from the Gaussian distribution for the binary classification case where we use the binary cross entropy it arises from the Bernoulli distribution. Importantly the common pattern between the two is that in both cases the error function is really just the negative log likelihood and therefore the solution we end up finding in the end is called the maximum likelihood solution.

So let's jump right in and try to figure out what this distribution is. In the case where we only have binary outcomes the correct discrete distribution is the Bernoulli distribution. So what is the correct distribution for multiple categorical outcomes. Well unlike the Gaussian and Bernoulli distributions this distribution is not named after a person. It is simply called quite appropriately the categorical distribution the usual analogy for the categorical distribution is a die roll. So when you roll a die. There are six possible outcomes. Typically one two three all the way up to six. Of course there are different kinds of dice. Well you may have even more possible outcomes. In general we will refer to the number of possible outcomes as K. So what does the categorical distribution look like. Well it looks a little strange as you can see it is a product each of the mu k's is a parameter telling us the probability that the result of the dice roll was k. In other words mu k is equal to the probability that x is equal to k. So what does this mean about the one function in the exponent. This is what is called an indicator function. It returns one and when its argument is true and 0 otherwise Knowing this it's easy to confirm that if we plug in x equals 1 We should get that the probability that x is equal to 1 equals mu 1. The probability that x is equal to 2 is mu 2 and so forth. In other words we can confirm that this is indeed the PMF for the categorical distribution as usual we are going to pretend we've collected N data points and we are going to do maximum likelihood estimation to find all the mus. What is interesting about this likelihood is that because the likelihood is the product of PMFs and the PMF already has a product we end up with two products in the likelihood also notice that there are two indices in the exponent here. There is the index i and also the index K so that should remind you of a matrix because a matrix also has two indices. The row in the column after taking the log. We know that we get the log likelihood and we already know that the negative log likelihood is our categorical cross entropy. So if we take the negative of this expression we will get back something that looks exactly like the categorical cross entropy and thus we can relate this back to our categorical cross entropy loss function. Notice here that it's a tiny bit different from our log likelihood and that we don't have an indicator function anymore. This is because an equivalent way of writing this is double indexing. y i k is called a one hot encoded value because it can only take on the values 1 or 0 each row can only have one 1. Remember that I represents the sample index and K represents the class label. The class label can only be one value. For example so for instance if I roll a die I can only get one number. It must be six or five or four three it can't be six and three at the same time so as another example if I have a picture and I'm classifying what type of animal it is it can only be one type of animal if it's a picture of a cat. It cannot simultaneously be a picture of a dog therefore only one of the K values can have a one representing the target. The rest of the values must be 0 you'll notice that one hot encoding the targets like this can be quite inefficient. Let's do a simple example. Suppose we have four samples so N is four and three classes cat dog or bird. Suppose the targets are cat dog bird and cat. So numerically we can represent this with the vector one two three one. But in order to one hot encode this vector we must turn it into a four by three matrix or an N by K matrix containing only zeros and ones. So the equivalent one hot encoding is 1 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 1 1 0 0. Now suppose my prediction probabilities also an n by K matrix are as follows. So for each sample and each class I have an associated probability it's the probability that I think the input belongs to that class after applying the categorical cross entropy formula. We get this value for the cost. Now you might be thinking that is a whole lot of multiplying by zero. We already know that anything multiplied by 0 0. So those values don't actually contribute anything to the cost. The only values that do matter are the ones which match the target. Remember the original target is the vector 1 2 3 1 What I would like to do ideally is to only take the log of these highlighted values and then add them altogether. The question is can I do that without one hot encoding the target first. And indeed this is possible in NumPy. We can use the double indexing trick NumPy arrays allow you to index using things such as lists and other arrays instead of just single integers. So if I wanted to take my predictions and index only the relevant values here's what I would do. I would take y hat at i equals 1 and k equals 1 I would take y hat at i equals 2 and k equals 2. I would take y hat at i equals 3 and k equals 3 and I would take y hat at i equals 4 and k equals 1 using the NumPy double indexing method. I can actually index all of these values at once I simply pass in all the row indices and the corresponding column indices at the same time. Importantly note that by doing this I never have to one hot encode the targets I can pass them directly into the square brackets as an exercise. You should try this in actual NumPy code to verify that it really works just note that in code we index starting at 0 instead of 1. And so this is the idea behind the sparse categorical cross entropy. So when you are in TensorFlow 2.0 if you use the regular categorical cross entropy you are using the one hot encoded target which requires n times K multiplications and additions. If you use the sparse categorical cross entropy you were using the original target which requires only n multiplications and additions. Therefore it's usually better to use the original target and apply the sparse categorical cross entropy loss.

But you are welcome to ask me about it on the Q and A Okay. This still doesn't answer the question why do we need a gradient descent. The answer is we use numerical approximations. One such example is finding integrals. Sometimes you can't solve for an integral by hand. So what's the idea behind gradient descent. The idea is if I take the gradient of the function with respect to the parameter W and I take small steps in that direction the value of the function will decrease. Provided that my step size is small enough eventually as I keep taking these very small steps I'm going to get closer and closer to the bottom of the curve. And eventually I will converge to an answer by converge I mean that when you get near the bottom your steps will become so small that they will become insignificant. So w doesn't change as you take more steps at that point. You have found the value of W that minimizes your function. So what does this look like in code. Basically it's just a for loop before the loop we initialize W to some random value then inside the loop we continually update w using the gradient descent formula so here's an example of gradient descent at work. Let's say we want to minimize w squared. So that's our loss function. The derivative is 2 W. So inside the loop we iteratively apply the equation W equals W minus eta times two times w. Now let's look at some code I've pasted that does this. As you can see I've initialized W to 5. In this lecture we are going to discuss stochastic gradient descent. Previously we looked at regular gradient descent and how it can be used to optimize a function. But as you may know in TensorFlow 2.0 the gradient descent option is called SGD which is short for stochastic gradient descent. So what makes it stochastic and how is it different from non stochastic gradient descent. To understand this let's first think of a simpler problem. Let's suppose we want to measure the average height of all humans in the entire world. Now that would be quite a hefty task. There are 7 billion people in the world and it would take a very long time to ask each person individually. But what if instead you took just one thousand random people and took the average height of these 1000 people would you expect the average height of these 1000 to be similar to the average height of the entire population. The answer is yes. It should be clear that the main advantage of asking only 1000 people instead of 7 billion people is that it would take much less time. OK so how is this relevant for deep learning. If you recall in deep learning we have to calculate the cost. And from this cost we have to calculate its gradient so that we can do a gradient descent. The problem is this cost depends on the number of training samples in our dataset. So imagine you are training on the famous ImageNet dataset which has about 1 million images. This means that for each iteration of your training loop you have to add up all the errors for all 1 million samples. That's going to take an extremely long time but what if instead I took the average error over just 1000 images. Of course they must be chosen randomly. The same idea applies this average error is probably close to the average error over the entire dataset and so if we do gradient descent using only these 1000 images we will probably end up taking a very similar step. Just with 1000 times less computation in actuality we typically use smaller batch sizes like 32 64 or 128. The basic algorithm looks like this instead of just one loop over the epochs we have two nested loops one over the epochs and one over the training set. The idea is we are going to split up our data into batches and for each batch we are going to take one step of gradient descent. As you can see in this pseudocode we are using a batch size of 32 so the number of iterations of the inner loop is n divided by 32. We can specify the start index as I times thirty two and the end index as I plus 1 times 32. So this will count from zero to thirty to thirty two to sixty four sixty four ninety six and so forth on each epoch we will make one pass through the entire dataset. It's important to randomize the data and each epoch because running through the same samples in the same order each time could lead to undesirable patterns being learned as an exercise. You may want to try this out for yourself to prove that it is faster to set up your experiment. Here's what you should do in the TensorFlow 2.0 fit function. You have an argument called batch size. You can take any of the examples from this course and explicitly set the batch size to a small value such as 32 and explicitly set it to the size of the entire dataset. Whatever that may be from there. Compare the time it takes for each method to converge to a minimum. You should find that with batch gradient descent. The training process converges much faster and in fact sometimes your dataset may be so large that doing one step of gradient descent cannot even fit into memory.

Everyone welcome back to this class modern Deep Learning in Python Deep Learning in Python. Part two in this lecture. We are going to look at what I consider to be one of the most effective improvements over plain gradient descent called momentum. Personally I found it to be the 80 percent factor that can improve your learning procedure. So how does momentum work. I like the analogy of a ball rolling down a hill which is nice because during gradient descent we imagine the error surface as the bottom of a hill. But I think today an even better analogy is moving something on a frictionless surface like ice. So if you've ever gone skating before you know that you can easily glide along the ice very quickly and without much force because the momentum just carries you the way you were going before you can imagine pushing a box on ice and the box will move from one point to another quite easily because you can push it once and it's going to slide. That's exactly what happens in physics. If there is no friction then an object will just continue to go in the direction it was already going of course ice still does have some friction. So eventually the box was slowed down and eventually stop as you'll see momentum in gradient descent also slows down after a while to to continue with this analogy. Let's try to think of a situation without momentum. Now keep in mind I'm talking about gradient descent momentum here not physics momentum since the definition of momentum and physics is a little different. So imagine now that instead of ice you're trying to push a box in sand. Now you can imagine that this is going to be very difficult because sand has lots of friction. So if you push a box in sand it's going to go as far as you push it and no more. If you want the box to move again you have to push it again. That's like gradient descent without momentum each time. If we want to move there has to be a gradient so that we can move in the direction of the gradient. Now let's try to put these ideas into math. Let's start with regular gradient descent without momentum. So we have theta at time t is equal to theta at time T minus one minus the learning rate times the gradient G. And from this we can see that if the gradient is zero nothing is going to happen to theta it just gets updated to its old value. It doesn't change now let's look at gradient descent with momentum. We use the term momentum very loosely here since it has nothing to do with actual physical momentum. So we create a new variable called V which stands for the velocity it's equal to mu times its old velocity minus the learning rate times the gradient. And this is exactly what we talked about earlier when we imagine pushing a box on ice. The G term is the effect of our pushing the box but the mu times V of T minus one term is the effect of continuing to move in the same direction as we were going before. Now we talked about how when you push a box on ice even though there's less friction and the box can slide it's still going to stop eventually. So we want the new V to take on only a fraction of the old V and so a typical value for mu which we also call the momentum term is zero point nine or zero point nine five or zero point nine nine. Somewhere in that area one thing you can immediately see is that if we plug in the expression for V of t we can get the update for theta of T in terms of only the old theta the old V and the gradient G. From here it's easy to see that if we set mu to zero we just get back regular old gradient descent. So what is the effect of using momentum. Well as you know in all of our scripts we like to plot the cost per iteration. And so what we usually see is that the cost converges to its minimum value much faster than if we had not used momentum. So using momentum is pretty great because it significantly speeds up training. Now I want to discuss one more perspective on momentum before we move on. This is what is typically taught in deep learning courses these days. So in this perspective the problem that momentum is solving is if we have unequal gradients in different directions. So for visualization purposes let's assume we have two parameters to optimize the vertical parameter and the horizontal parameter. So the gradient in one direction is very steep and the gradient in the other direction is very shallow. The idea is if you don't have momentum then you rely purely on the gradient which points more in the steep direction than in the shallow direction. And this is just a property of the gradient. It's the direction of steepest descent. So since this gradient vector points more in the steep direction than the result is we're going to zigzag back and forth across this valley. And that's a really inefficient way of reaching the minimum. So what happens when we add momentum to this situation. Well since in the shallow direction we move in the same direction every time those velocities are going to accumulate. So we'll have a portion of our old velocity added to our new velocity to help us along in that direction. The result is that we get there faster by taking bigger steps in the direction of the shallow gradient.
